activity: how a poll's margin of error and sample size limit what its numbers can say
knowledge_domain: how a poll's margin of error and sample size limit what its numbers can say
fact: A poll's stated margin of error applies to each candidate's share; the margin of error for the lead between two candidates is about twice as large.
story:
The fluorescent light above the layout table flickered twice before it settled, and Natalie took that as a sign to stop pretending she wasn't staring at the printout. The Ridgefield High Courier had polled 300 students on the student council election, and Eden had already written the headline: CHAVEZ LEADS REYES BY FOUR. The issue went to the printer at nine p.m., and it was already seven-forty.

"Read it again," Eden said, not looking up from her screen. She was the paper's raconteur, the one who could turn a cafeteria menu change into a two-thousand-word saga, and she wrote headlines the way she told stories, with total conviction. "Chavez forty-six, Reyes forty-two. Four-point lead. Margin of error three points. That's outside the margin. She's winning."

"Outside the margin," Jada repeated from the doorway, dropping her backpack on the couch. She'd come from cross-country practice and her hair was still wet. "That's what my brother said too."

Natalie turned the printout over, as if the back might contain something the front had hidden. It didn't. She'd taken statistics second period with Mr. Russo, and something about Eden's certainty was snagging on a lesson she'd half ignored, something he'd said while she was sublimating her boredom into elaborate margin doodles. The margin of error applied to each candidate's share. She remembered writing that down. Each share. Not the gap between them.

"Eden, wait." She pulled the calculator across the table, though the arithmetic barely needed one. "If Chavez's forty-six could really be forty-three, and Reyes's forty-two could really be forty-five."

"Then it's a tie," Eden said. "So what? It could also be forty-nine to thirty-nine."

"No, that's the point. It could be a lot of things." Natalie spread her hands over the printout. "The margin on each number is three. But the margin on the lead, the difference, is about twice that. So a four-point lead with a three-point margin of error isn't a sure thing. The real margin on the lead is closer to six."

Jada sat down slowly. "Twice?"

"About twice," Natalie said, and she was careful with that word, careful because Mr. Russo had been careful with it, and because she was aware that she was building an argument on a doodle-adjacent memory. "The stated margin applies to each candidate's share. For the lead between them, it's about twice as large."

Eden finally looked up. Outside, the parking lot had gone dark except for one sodium lamp near the gym, and the room felt smaller under it, the three of them and the flickering tube and a headline that had been true an hour ago in a different way. "So what do we print? 'Chavez Maybe Leads Reyes, We Honestly Can't Tell'?"

"Something like that, actually." Natalie pulled a chair over. "Or we don't headline the lead at all. We headline the turnout number. Eighty-one percent said they'd actually vote, that's up from fifty last year. That's not close. That's the story."

"You want to bury the election," Eden said.

"I want to bury a number that might be a coin flip."

They argued for twenty minutes, the way they argued about everything, fast and without cruelty. Eden said readers wanted a winner; Natalie said readers wanted the truth and would forgive a smaller truth more readily than a wrong one. Jada mostly listened, spinning a highlighter on the table, until she finally said, "My brother's poll in college had the same problem. They printed the wrong guy ahead and he lost by two points and everyone blamed the paper."

That settled it more than any of Natalie's arithmetic. Eden deleted the headline at 8:31 and typed a new one, grumbling that Natalie had turned the cosmopolitan Courier into a statistics journal, which was a generous description of a paper that ran twelve pages and mostly reviewed horror movies. The new headline read CHAVEZ AHEAD, RACE TIGHT; TURNOUT EXPECTED TO SURGE. It wasn't exciting. Natalie found she preferred it that way, though she noticed, as Eden hit send on the final pages, that she still wasn't sure. The poll had talked to 300 students out of 1,400, and even the turnout number carried its own margin she hadn't calculated.

Mr. Russo appeared in the doorway at 8:55, holding his keys, apparently the last teacher in the building. "You're cutting it close," he said.

"Natalie made us rewrite the headline," Eden said. "Something about the margin being twice as big."

Mr. Russo looked at Natalie, one eyebrow up, and she braced for a lecture. Instead he just said, "Good," and jingled his keys toward the hall. "Lock up when you're done."

Jada gathered her backpack. Eden closed her laptop and stood for a moment at the window, watching the sodium lamp, and then she said, "If Reyes wins by one point, you're writing the retraction yourself." Natalie was still laughing when she turned off the flickering light.

activity: to analyse a population pyramid to predict whether a country will need more schools or nursing homes
knowledge_domain: to analyse a population pyramid to predict whether a country will need more schools or nursing homes
fact: A population pyramid conventionally shows males on the left and females on the right, with age groups stacked from youngest at the bottom to oldest at the top.
story:
The tent pole had bent on the second night, so by the third morning Lucas was eating instant oatmeal under a tarp with the pages Ms. Hassan had assigned spread across his sleeping bag like a map of a country he would never visit. "Population structure of Sweden," the handout said, and then that strange graph, two stacks of bars leaning away from each other like a couple arguing. He held it close to the camp stove's warmth and frowned. Prince, still in his mummy bag with only his face showing, said, "You look like a man being defeated by paper."

"Ms. Hassan wants us to say whether the country needs more schools or more nursing homes," Lucas said. "I've been reading it backwards, I think. I assumed the left side was females." He tilted the page, then tilted his head to match it. Alyson, who had been drying mugs with obdurate efficiency since dawn, leaned over his shoulder without asking, which was her way.

"It's the other way," she said. "Males on the left, females on the right." She tapped the bottom bars. "And the ages go youngest at the bottom, oldest at the top. It stacks upward, like your granddad's birthday cake if he were a hundred."

"So the wide part at the bottom is the young people," Lucas said slowly, and something rearranged itself in his head with a small, satisfying click, the kind of click he usually only got from a locker finally yielding. For Kenya, the second handout, the bottom of the pyramid flared out enormously, a city of children, and the top narrowed to almost nothing. For Japan the base had pinched itself thin and the middle bulged like a river dammed upstream. He laid the two pages side by side on the pine needles.

"Kenya," he announced, "is going to need a lot of schools."

"Congratulations," Prince said from inside his bag. "You have counted the children. Would you like a medal, or a second medal?"

"You don't get it. Look, the shape tells you the future. All these kids at the bottom are going to be adults, and then there'll be even more kids under them, unless something changes. Japan has this skinny base, which means fewer young people coming up to take care of the wide old part at the top." He traced the Japanese pyramid's sides with one finger, up and up, past the bulge of the middle-aged, to the sparse bars at the very top where the oldest lived. "Nursing homes. Or immigration. Or robots, maybe."

Alyson sat down on a cooler, mug still in hand, and looked at him with an interest she did not usually waste on mornings. "So which is better? To be Kenya or Japan?"

"That's a trap question," Lucas said. "It's like asking whether it's better to be hungry or tired." He thought about it while a jay screamed at them from the oak above the stove. There was something he was circling, something about how the same graph could be read as a problem or as a promise depending on who was doing the reading. His economics teacher back home liked to valorize growth, always growth, as if a widening base were the only shape a good country could take. But a wide base meant classrooms to build and jobs to find and, eventually, an even wider base. A narrow base meant comfort now and shortage later. Neither shape was a verdict; both were a bet on the future that the future had not yet agreed to.

"That's not an answer," Alyson said.

"It's the honest one. I can tell you what the graph shows. I can't tell you what the country should want." He picked up the Kenya page again and felt a strange exhilaration, looking at all those children stacked in their blue and pink bars, an entire generation arriving whether anyone had planned for them or not. Somewhere in that shape were schools that hadn't been built yet.

Ms. Hassan's whistle sounded from the trail, two short blasts meaning pack up. Prince unzipped his bag at last, blinking like something newly hatched, and started stuffing the tent into its sack with total disregard for its geometry. Lucas folded the two pyramids together, Kenya inside Japan, wrong sides out, and carried them to the fire to show her. "Ms. Hassan," he said, "I have a finding, a caveat, and a question, in that order."

activity: to write a critical review comparing two scholarly articles on the same question
knowledge_domain: to write a critical review comparing two scholarly articles on the same question
fact: A p-value is the probability of getting results at least as extreme as those observed if there were truly no effect; it is not the probability that the hypothesis is true.
story:
Ava had promised herself she would start the review on Friday, and it was now Sunday evening, and the two articles lay open on the kitchen table like patients no one wanted to treat. Both asked the same question, whether delaying high school start times improved grades, and both had reached opposite conclusions, and Mr. Ortiz had said in class that a good review would not simply pick a winner but weigh what each study could actually show. Her mother kept passing through the kitchen with laundry, and each time she paused at the table long enough to set down a glass of water or a plate of crackers, as if food were the only help she could legally offer at this hour.

The first article, the one with the positive result, reported a p-value of 0.05 and trumpeted its finding in the abstract. The second found nothing and grumbled about sample sizes. Ava had underlined the number three times and written in the margin of her notebook, ninety-five percent, which felt like a solid thing to build a paragraph around. She typed a sentence: the first study's results were 95 percent likely to be correct. Then she sat back and looked at it, because somewhere behind it a small doubt was ticking like a watch under a pillow.

She texted Ryan, who had done the statistics unit last semester and lorded it over everyone. He answered on the third ring of the call, his voice tinny above the sound of his little brother's cartoon. "Read me the sentence," he said, and she did, and there was a pause long enough for her to regret the whole evening. "Where did you get ninety-five percent?" he asked. "It's right there. P equals 0.05. Five percent chance the study's wrong, so ninety-five percent chance it's right." Ryan laughed, not unkindly, which somehow made it worse. "That's not what a p-value is. I don't remember the exact wording, though. Look it up before you write another word."

She looked it up. The screen glowed back at her and she read the definition three times, slowly, the way you reread a text message that changes your plans. Then she copied it into her notebook word for word, because she did not trust her own paraphrase yet: a p-value is the probability of getting results at least as extreme as those observed if there were truly no effect; it is not the probability that the hypothesis being true. She underlined the last clause twice. All those weeks she had carried the number around like a coin she assumed she knew the value of, and it turned out to be currency from a different country. The first study's p-value of 0.05 was not a grade. It was a statement about what the world would look like if the effect were not there at all.

Her mother drifted past again and stopped, genuinely stopped this time, the laundry basket on her hip. "You look like you've seen a ghost," she said. "Worse. I've seen my own draft." Her mother laughed and set an orange beside the crackers, an offering to a temple she didn't worship at, and Ava felt a small, unpayable debt of gratitude. She peeled it while she reread both articles, and the citrus smell sharpened her somehow, the way Mr. Ortiz claimed a change of setting did, and she began to see the shape of what she could honestly write. The two studies were not simply disagreeing, like two witnesses telling different stories about the same crash. They were answering different questions and reporting different numbers whose meanings she had only now learned to hold correctly.

She called Parsa, who was awake because Parsa was always awake. "Can I say something at you and you tell me if it sounds insane?" Parsa said that was practically her hobby, so Ava said it: "The p-value is the probability of getting results at least as extreme as the ones they observed if there were truly no effect. It is not the probability that the hypothesis is true." Parsa was quiet for a moment. "Say the first part again." Ava said it again. "So the number isn't about whether the thing is real at all." "Right. It's about the data, given a world where nothing's happening." She could hear Parsa's chair creak on the other end. "That's kind of beautiful, actually. It's like the study is describing a shadow instead of the object." Ava laughed, and wrote shadow in the margin, and thought that Parsa should perhaps be paid for this.

It was past eleven when she started the real draft. She wrote that the first study's small p-value told her the results would be surprising in a world with no effect, and that this was worth something, but it was not the five-alarm conclusion the abstract implied. She wrote that the second study's null result didn't prove the absence of an effect any more than the first proved its presence, and that a reader caught between them needed to hold both uncertainties at once. Somewhere in the third paragraph she typed that science was less like a verdict and more like a court still hearing evidence, then deleted it, because it was the kind of sentence that wanted to be admired more than it wanted to be true. She was grateful to Ryan for catching her, and she made a mental note to say so in person tomorrow, in the hallway, where gratitude was harder to fake.

At twelve-forty she saved the file, and it was not finished, and it was honest, and she could not yet tell which of those two facts mattered more to Mr. Ortiz, who would collect it at eight in the morning. Her mother had left the kitchen light on for her, the way she always did, an altruistic smallness that Ava suspected she would not properly notice until she was much older and paying her own electric bill. Ava closed the laptop, turned off the light, and stood a moment in the dark. Somewhere in her notebook, beside carbon and graphite, Mr. Ortiz had written once that the same element could be two different things depending on how it was arranged, an allotrope of the truth, and she thought about the number 0.05, which was one thing in the abstract and another thing entirely on her kitchen table. She went upstairs, and the stairs did not creak, and through Ryan's window across the street, a lamp was still burning too.

activity: to compare two apartment leases and work out the total monthly cost including utilities
knowledge_domain: to compare two apartment leases and work out the total monthly cost including utilities
fact: A lease that says 'utilities included' may cover only some utilities; the lease wording decides which, so each utility has to be checked separately.
story:
Nathan spread the two leases across the kitchen table and weighted their corners with the salt cellar and his mother's mug, still warm. The first was for a studio above the laundromat on Creighton Street, four hundred dollars a month, utilities included. The second was a shared two-bedroom with Hiba, three hundred each, plus electricity and heat. He had assumed, until this morning, that the studio was obviously cheaper, the way a closed door is obviously a wall.

Hiba came in through the back door without knocking, the way she had since they were eleven, and set a bag of clementines on the counter. "Tell me the studio is worse," she said. "I already measured my desk for the corner bedroom. It fits with room for a chair." She wanted the answer to come out a certain way, and they both knew it, and she sat down anyway.

"Utilities included," Nathan read aloud, and then turned the page and read further, because his mother had taught him that the large print giveth. Buried in paragraph eleven was a list: water included, trash included, heat included. Electricity was not on the list. He read the paragraph twice. "Utilities included," he said slowly, "but only some utilities. The lease wording decides which. So you have to check each one separately." Electricity, in their town, in an old building with baseboard heating, was not a small thing.

"You sound like a lawyer," Hiba said, but she peeled a clementine and leaned in. She had her own money problem, the one she hadn't said out loud yet: her father had lost hours at the plant in March, and the three hundred a month was already a stretch she hadn't told him about. Nathan could see her doing the arithmetic behind her eyes, though the arithmetic was not the kind you could check.

He called the utility company and asked the cashier's question, the boring one, what an apartment like that ran in winter, and wrote the number on the back of an envelope. Then he added it. The studio came to more than the shared place in the cold months, less in the warm ones, and the total depended on a winter nobody had lived through yet. He told her that, plainly. "It's close," he said. "I can't make it exact."

Katie arrived halfway through, drawn by the smell of the kettle, and looked over their shoulders with the jaundiced expression she reserved for anything involving landlords. "They'll get you somehow," she said. "It's always in the fine print." Nathan didn't argue. He had nearly signed the studio on the strength of two words on the first page, and the memory of his own certainty embarrassed him more than Katie's skepticism did. His old way of thinking had been fast, the door-is-a-wall way. The new way was slower, more asceticism than cleverness: read every line, check every utility, assume nothing is included until the lease says so. He didn't love the slowness. It had, though, catalyzed something like respect between him and the documents, and between him and Hiba, who was watching him now with less hurry.

"Even if the studio were cheaper," she said, and stopped. She pulled the skin off another clementine in one long spiral, which she only did when she was deciding something. "My dad's hours got cut. I'd need the rent to stay at three hundred, maybe less some months. I should have told you before you did all this." The room got quiet in the way it does when someone has finally said the true thing. Nathan looked at the two leases, at the numbers he had spent the afternoon assembling, and understood that the numbers were only part of what he'd been comparing.

They stayed at the table while the kettle went cold. He marked the electricity clause in the studio lease with a yellow highlighter, then wrote a list of questions for the landlord, one per utility, and a second list for the two-bedroom, because "plus electricity and heat" might mean exactly that or something looser, and he had learned not to trust a phrase's manners. Hiba took half the clementines and said she'd ask her cousin, who had lived above the laundromat, about the winter bills. Katie boiled the kettle again without being asked.

Nathan folded both leases into his backpack, one in each pocket so they couldn't mix. He was honest with himself on the walk to the door: he still didn't know which apartment won, and the winter bills would decide it in a language he couldn't read until spring. But he had the questions now, written in his own handwriting, and a phone number for a landlord who answered on the second ring. He called from the kitchen doorway, and when the man picked up, Nathan said, "Hi, I'm looking at the studio on Creighton. I want to go through the utilities one by one."

activity: cooking or baking a meal for the family
knowledge_domain: cooking or baking a meal for the family
fact: Mise en place is a French cooking term meaning 'putting in place': measuring and preparing all the ingredients before starting to cook.
story:
The grill was already hot when Jake spread the recipe across the picnic table and weighted its corners with stones. He had promised his mother a full dinner before she got home from her shift: smoked chicken, grilled corn, and a cornbread she had once said reminded her of her own mother's kitchen. The backyard had become his for the afternoon. His father was at work, his sister at practice, and the neighbor's dog had settled under the fence in the strip of shade it claimed every day at four.

He measured the cornmeal into a bowl, then the flour, then the sugar, and stirred them together with a wooden spoon gone pale from years of washing. The recipe said to whisk in two eggs and melted butter, then pour everything into the skillet and slide it onto the grill's cool side. He opened the refrigerator door that stuck unless you lifted it slightly, and looked at the shelf where the eggs should have been. There was a jar of pickles, half an onion in plastic wrap, and a carton of milk with two days left on it. No eggs.

He checked the garage refrigerator, which held only his father's drinks and a bag of walnuts nobody ate. He checked the cooler by the shed. Then he stood in the middle of the yard with his phone in his hand, the dry ingredients sitting in their bowl behind him, and texted Abel, who had spent the whole summer working the line at a restaurant across town.

Abel called him instead of texting back. "Tell me you didn't mix it already."

"I mixed the dry stuff. The wet stuff goes in last."

There was a pause on the line, the sound of a kitchen behind Abel, someone calling out orders. "You're cooking blind, man. At work we do this thing, mise en place. It's French. It means putting in place. Everything measured and prepped before you even turn on a flame."

"So I've heard of it and failed it in the same afternoon."

"Basically. Do you have any eggs at all?"

Jake said he didn't, and Abel said he couldn't leave for another hour, and then they hung up, and Jake stood there doing the arithmetic of the evening. His mother would be home at six-thirty. The chicken needed an hour on the grill plus rest. The cornbread, by the recipe's clock, needed forty minutes. He could abandon the cornbread, or he could find two eggs somewhere in the next twenty minutes, because the chicken couldn't wait for him to be philosophical about it.

He climbed the low fence into Ms. Goh's yard, where she was deadheading her roses with small silver scissors. He had known her since he was seven, when she had extended a kind of standing clemency toward the balls and rockets that came over that fence, returning them without complaint and once without comment even when a water balloon had caught her squarely in the shoulder. He asked her, a little out of breath, whether she had eggs.

"Two," she said. "That's all I have until my shop tomorrow. What are they underwriting, this theft of mine?"

"Dinner," Jake said. "My mother's birthday. I'm making cornbread and I already mixed everything else, and then I found out we don't have any, which apparently is the exact mistake there's a whole French term for."

Ms. Goh went inside and came back with the two eggs wrapped in a dish towel, and she handed them over with the ceremony of someone releasing hostages. "In my family," she said, "the birthday person was never allowed in the kitchen. My father said it was bad luck to see your own cake before it existed."

"My mom's not allowed in mine either," Jake said. "It's not luck, it's just that she'll start helping and then it's her dinner and not mine."

She laughed at that, a short, genuine sound, and shooed him back over the fence.

Back at the picnic table he cracked the eggs into a cup, one and then the other, and watched the yolks hold their shape. He melted the butter in the skillet over the grill's hot side, poured the wet into the dry, and folded the batter with fewer strokes than felt natural, because the recipe had said not to overmix, and he was finished with ignoring recipes. The skillet went to the cool side. He closed the lid and checked his phone: 5:12. Enough time, if nothing else went missing.

While the cornbread baked he sat on the back step and texted Abel a photograph of the skillet with steam rising off it, no caption. Abel replied with a single thumbs-up and then, a minute later, "mise en place next time." Jake looked out at the yard, at the dog still flopped in its strip of shade, at the smoke threading up from the grill into a sky that was starting to go the color of the inside of a peach. He thought about how he had planned the whole meal around what his mother would love and had somehow never once opened the refrigerator to check what was in it, and he decided that both things could be true, that he had been careful and careless at once, and that he would not know until she tasted it which one had mattered more.

At 5:40 he lifted the lid and pressed the cornbread's center with his finger. It sprang back. He carried the skillet to the table using the dish towel Ms. Goh had forgotten to take back, set it down among the stones, and went inside to wash his hands for the chicken. Through the window he heard his sister's car in the driveway, and he called out, without turning around, "Nobody touches the bread."

activity: to give honest feedback to a teammate in a way that is specific and kind
knowledge_domain: to give honest feedback to a teammate in a way that is specific and kind
fact: In a 2014 study led by David Yeager, students were more likely to revise essays when critical comments came with a note saying the teacher had high standards and believed they could meet them.
story:
The kitchen table at Christophe's house still had the ring stains from somebody's coffee mugs, and Christophe's essay lay between them like a patient nobody wanted to operate on. Alex had promised to read it, and he had read it, twice, on the bus over, and the problems were not mysterious. The middle paragraphs drifted. The argument about flood insurance in coastal towns started three separate times without ever landing a claim. Christophe, who wanted this essay for a scholarship application, needed to hear all of it.

"Is it good?" Christophe asked. He was folding a napkin into smaller and smaller squares, which he did when he was nervous, a habit Alex had watched since seventh grade.

"It's not bad," Alex said, and hated himself a little, because that was the kind of sentence that meant nothing. It was the verbal equivalent of patting someone's shoulder while looking at the door.

Carla was at the counter making tea, and she turned around with the spoon still in the mug. "You just did the thing," she said. "The thing where you soften it until it disappears."

"I softened it because he's my friend."

"He's my friend too," Carla said. "That's the reason to be clear, not the reason to be vague." She set the mug down and pulled out her phone, scrolling through photos until she found a screenshot of a page from her psych class. "Look at this. In a 2014 study led by David Yeager, students were way more likely to revise their essays when the critical comments came with a note saying the teacher had high standards and believed they could reach them."

Alex read the screenshot twice. Christophe leaned over his shoulder to read it too, and for a moment the essay on the table was forgotten. "So the note is what did it," Christophe said slowly. "Not the comment itself."

"That's what it says," Carla said. "The comment plus the belief. Together."

Alex sat back. He thought about Mr. Oyelaran, who coached their debate team and who had a way of saying "this is below what you can do" that somehow felt like a door opening rather than one closing. Alex had always assumed it was a personality, a talent you either had or didn't. Now he wondered if it was a method, something with moving parts you could study. The distinction mattered to him. If kindness and honesty were a personality, he was out of luck, because his natural instinct was clearly to blur the hard thing until it evaporated. If they were a method, he could practice.

"You have high standards," Carla said to him, watching his face. "So say that part out loud, and then say the real feedback. Don't titrate the criticism down to nothing. Titrate the kindness up."

"That's the most Carla sentence you've ever said," Christophe said, but he was smiling a little, unfolding his napkin.

"You can't just argue about semantics," Carla said. "There's a real difference between 'it's not bad' and 'this is good and it needs work.' Those aren't the same sentence wearing different hats."

Alex pulled the essay toward himself and found the paragraph about the floodplain maps with his finger. "Okay. Christophe, I think you can win this scholarship, and I think this essay is below what you're capable of. So here's the specific thing. Your third paragraph starts the whole argument over. You introduce the maps, then you introduce them again two paragraphs later, and the second introduction is better. Cut the first one. Start there." He kept going while his nerve held. The sentence about premiums buried the point; the conclusion arrived before the evidence; the anecdote about the mayor was good and belonged at the top. Some of it came out clumsier than he'd rehearsed on the bus, and he caught himself hedging twice and had to unsay the hedges.

Christophe wrote nothing down for the first minute, just listened, and Alex could not read his face, which terrified him. Then Christophe picked up a pen, drew a line through the first introduction, and wrote "move mayor up" in the margin. "The premiums thing," he said. "You're right. I was avoiding it because I couldn't make it clear." He looked at the essay, then at Alex. "Say the belief part again."

"I think you can win it."

Christophe nodded once and started crossing things out. At the counter, Carla raised her mug toward Alex like a small toast, and the afternoon light moved across the ruined, improving page.

activity: to direct a one-act play by blocking the actors' movements and running rehearsals
knowledge_domain: to direct a one-act play by blocking the actors' movements and running rehearsals
fact: Stage left and stage right are named from the actor's point of view while facing the audience, so they are the reverse of the audience's left and right.
story:
On Monday Ms. Carvalho handed Robert a clipboard and told him the one-act had to be performance-ready by Friday, because the auditorium was booked for a robotics banquet on Saturday. The play was his own, twelve pages he had written in October, and he had assumed until that moment that directing it would be the easy part.

He had three actors and a gym stage with taped lines from badminton courts crossing it diagonally. Alysha played the sister, Judy played the neighbour, and a sophomore whose name Robert kept forgetting played the brother. For the first rehearsal he stood at the folding table he'd dragged to the edge of the stage and read his own stage directions aloud. "Judy, enter left, cross to the table, put the letter down."

Judy walked to the other side of the stage.

"No, your left," Robert said, and she stopped, turned halfway around, and looked at him with the patience of someone deciding whether he was joking.

"Stage left is the actor's left," Judy said. "Facing the audience. So it's that side."

Robert looked down at his script. He had written "left" four times and "right" twice, and he had never once considered whose left he meant. His own, obviously, since he had imagined the whole play from the fifth row, where he sat when he read it over. He crossed out the directions and wrote in "stage left" and "stage right," and then, because the audience's left and right were the reverse, he drew a little diagram in the margin so he would not have to think it through again every time.

The blocking came slowly after that. Alysha argued that her second monologue should be delivered downstage, close to the audience, and Robert wanted her further back, near the window that was only a painted flat. They tried it both ways. Downstage, the speech was louder and more immediate; upstage, she seemed to be talking to the room rather than to the seats, and Robert found he believed her more, though he could not have said why. He told her to keep it upstage. She shrugged and marked it in her script with a pencil she kept behind her ear.

By Wednesday the sophomore still could not land his entrance. He came in a beat late every time, then apologized, then came in late again. Robert wanted to be the kind of director who did not raise his voice, and he also wanted the entrance on time, and he discovered these were competing loyalties. He sublimated the impulse to snap into a faster cue line, calling the offstage prompt a half-second earlier, and it worked twice before the sophomore caught on and glared at him through the painted window.

Thursday night they ran the whole thing for Ms. Carvalho, who sat in the third row with her coat still on. The run had a strange, suspended quality, the half hour between a rehearsal and a performance, and Robert thought that this liminality was the part of theatre nobody warned you about, the stretch where the play was no longer his pages and not yet anyone's show. Ms. Carvalho made three notes and gave them to him folded in half. The second note said the pacing in the kitchen scene was obdurate, that the brother and sister were talking past each other on purpose but the audience needed to see the pulse underneath.

Robert read the note in the hallway afterward. His instinct was that the scene was cold on purpose, that the siblings' refusal to meet each other's eyes was the whole point, and that slowing it down to show feeling would soften what he had built. But Ms. Carvalho had been watching from the audience, from the direction his whole script had been accidentally facing, and he had learned this week that his own point of view was not the same as everyone else's. He was not sure whether the note was right. He was not sure whether uncertainty was a failure of conviction or the beginning of judgment.

Friday at lunch he called the three actors together. He kept the coldness in the kitchen scene, because he believed in it, but he gave Judy one new move: when Alysha says the line about the winter, Judy was to stop, stage left, and look at her for two full seconds before crossing. It was a compromise between what he wanted and what he'd been told, and he could not have defended it except that when they ran it, the whole scene changed temperature by exactly one degree.

At four o'clock the auditorium doors opened and ninety people came in, more than he expected, and Robert stood in the wings, stage left, holding his clipboard. Judy waited beside him in the dark, breathing in time with the house lights going down. The lights came up on the empty kitchen, and from where Robert stood, everything was reversed.

activity: to explain how greenhouse gases trap heat and read a graph of carbon dioxide over the last century
knowledge_domain: to explain how greenhouse gases trap heat and read a graph of carbon dioxide over the last century
fact: Methane traps far more heat per molecule than carbon dioxide, but a methane molecule stays in the atmosphere for only about a decade on average, much less time than carbon dioxide.
story:
The climate wing of the science museum smelled like floor wax and recycled air, and Paige had been standing in front of the carbon dioxide graph for eleven minutes. The line began in 1958, when a man on a Hawaiian volcano started measuring the sky, and it climbed in a shallow, steady sawtooth, dipping each summer and rising each winter, higher every year than the year before. She was supposed to be able to explain this to eighth graders on Saturday. She was a volunteer docent now, which meant she had to sound like she understood it, and she was not sanguine about her chances. The number at the far right of the graph was larger than the number at the left by more than a third, and she knew that meant something, and she did not yet know how to say what.

She had taken the job because Savanna had dared her to, in the way that friends dare you toward things they secretly want for you. Mostly it involved refilling the rubbing alcohol at the cloud-chamber table. But Saturday was the school group, and the school group got the full tour, greenhouse effect and all, and Mr. Farah, who ran the volunteer program, had looked at her signup sheet and said, "You'll do fine," with a confidence she found embarrassing.

Behind her, two voices rose over the hum of the exhibits. Sebastien was pointing at a wall panel titled Where the Extra Heat Goes, and Savanna had her arms crossed in the way she did when she was about to win an argument. "It's methane," Savanna was saying. "If you want to actually slow warming in the next few years, you fix methane leaks. Everyone says so."

"It's carbon dioxide," Sebastien said. "That's the whole graph. That's the whole wall."

Paige drifted over. The panel they were fighting about showed two molecules, CO2 drawn as three balls, CH4 as five, and a short paragraph underneath in small print. She read it twice while they kept talking over her shoulder. "Methane traps far more heat per molecule," she read out loud, slowly, "but a methane molecule stays in the atmosphere for only about a decade on average. Much less time than carbon dioxide." She looked up. "So you're both right. Kind of."

"Kind of is not an answer," Savanna said.

But Paige was staring at the panel, working it through. If methane was gone in ten years or so, then stopping the leaks would matter soon, in the window her friend kept talking about, while carbon dioxide just kept sitting there, decade after decade, the whole sawtooth line of it. "If you cut methane now," she said, "the stuff already up there fades out on its own inside about ten years. If you cut carbon dioxide now, what's up there mostly stays. So for the next few years, methane's the faster lever." She hesitated. "I think. For the short run."

Sebastien had gone quiet, which for Sebastien was a kind of concession. What he saw, standing there with his hands in the pockets of his jacket, was Paige reading the panel a third time, mouthing the numbers, her finger hovering an inch off the glass as though the print might smudge. He had spent the bus ride lambasting the museum's sponsors, some amalgam of oil money and municipal funding that he found indefensible, and he was a little ashamed of it now, because she was doing the thing he only talked about: actually learning the material, molecule by molecule, until she could stand in front of children and say it plainly. He turned and walked toward the cloud chamber and watched the white streaks thread through the alcohol fog, particles nobody could see becoming visible because somebody had built the right box.

That night Paige sat on her bed with the training binder open to the CO2 graph, which she had photocopied at the library for ten cents. The sawtooth looked different on paper, flatter, less alarming, and she wondered whether the museum had chosen the wall version precisely because the steepness frightened people into paying attention. She believed in frightening people a little. She also believed it was a kind of lying, depending on the axis. She held both beliefs at once and could not get them to sit still together.

Her phone buzzed against her hip. A message from Savanna: "ok i looked it up more. decade average for methane, that part was on your wall panel too. so i'm right for the next few years and sebastien is right for the century???" Paige typed back: "basically yes." Then, after a minute: "i'm going to tell the eighth graders both parts. fast lever and slow lever." Savanna replied with a single thumbs up, and then a second message: "you sound like a docent already." Paige put the phone face down on the comforter and went back to the graph, tracing the summer dips with the cap of her pen, the whole planet inhaling and exhaling while the line climbed anyway.

Saturday came cold and bright. The eighth graders arrived in a rattling yellow bus, thirty-one of them, louder than the HVAC. Paige walked them to the wall with the graph, and when a girl in a green hoodie asked why the line wiggled, Paige told her about the breathing of the northern forests, and the girl said, "Oh," in a voice that made the wiggle suddenly worth everything. At the methane panel, Paige gave them both levers, the fast one and the slow one, and did not pretend to know which one the world would choose to pull. A boy asked her if it was too late, and she said, "I don't know," and watched his face to see whether the honesty helped or hurt. He nodded slowly, still looking at the graph.

After the group left, Mr. Farah came down the corridor with his clipboard and asked how it had gone. Paige looked past him at the wall, at the small print about the decade, at the climbing line. "Can I take the Saturday group again next month?" she said.

activity: to compose a sixteen-bar melody with chord changes and write it in standard notation
knowledge_domain: to compose a sixteen-bar melody with chord changes and write it in standard notation
fact: In C major the dominant seventh chord is G7, made of the notes G, B, D and F, and it pulls strongly toward the C major chord.
story:
The concert hall smelled of dust and lemon polish, and the stage lights made the empty rows of red seats glow like something underwater. Maika sat in the third row with her staff paper on a clipboard, sixteen bars of a melody that still refused to end. Fifteen bars worked. The sixteenth kept collapsing, soft and unfinished, like a sentence trailing off so nobody would notice it had no conclusion. Around her, eleven other students from the young composers' day sharpened pencils and whispered. In twenty minutes the small ensemble upstairs would read every submitted score straight through, and the rules on the board said it plainly: whatever was on the page at three o'clock was what would be played.

She had written the melody for her grandmother, who hummed while she cooked and could not read a note of music. That part had come easily, a rising figure that wandered like a voice calling from another room. The chord changes under it were the hard part. Ms. Morales had told them at the morning session that a melody without harmony was like a face without expression, and had then refused to say anything more useful than that, which Maika had found beautiful at the time and now found outrageous.

Agathe was two rows ahead, and had already turned her pages face down in a neat stack, done, smug, indifferent. Aydan slid into the seat beside Maika and looked at the clipboard without asking. "Bar fifteen," he said. "What happens there?"

"Nothing happens there. That's the problem." She played the ending against the armrest, quietly, her fingers on the wood. The last chord was C under the melody, whole and plain, and it should have felt like arriving home. Instead it felt like walking into a house where the furniture had been sold.

Aydan leaned back and said nothing, which was his way of being both kind and useless. Above them, the ensemble finished tuning. The violist plucked her open strings one last time, a sound like water dripping, and the audience of students settled.

The first reading was Agathe's. Her melody was showy and a little cold, all leaps and display, but at the second-to-last bar something happened that Maika sat forward for. One note was added to the chord, and the whole final chord after it seemed to lean toward it, then land. The room actually reacted, a soft exhale across the rows. Agathe turned around to see who had noticed. Maika raised her hand slightly, not to congratulate her, but because she had recognized something, the way you recognize a person's walk before you see their face.

Afterward she caught Agathe in the aisle. "The chord before the end," Maika said. "What was it?"

Agathe considered her for a moment, deciding how much to enfranchise a rival with. "G7," she said. "G, B, D and F." Then she added, with the faint reluctance of someone handing over a key, "It pulls strongly toward C major." She walked off toward the stage to collect her score.

Maika sat back down. In C major, the dominant seventh. She looked at her own bar fifteen, the plain G chord she had written there, the melody note sitting on top of it like a hat on the wrong head. One note. She could hear it before she wrote it, an F sharpening the chord into something that wanted, that reached, that could not stay. Her pencil hovered. The conductor was announcing the second piece, someone's leitmotif exercise, a small tune that returned in every section like a guest who kept coming back. There was time. There was almost time. Her page still had to go up to the music stand, and the pages had already been collected once, and she would have to walk the corrected sheet to the front herself, past the vestigial ticket booth nobody staffed anymore, in front of everyone.

She wrote the F in, small and certain, in the space below the chord. Then she stood, and the clip of her pencil rolling off the clipboard and onto the floor was louder than she expected, so that half the room turned. She picked it up, walked up the centre aisle, and handed the page to the violist, who glanced at the fresh graphite and gave her a look that held a whole conversation about deadlines and mercy. The conductor tapped his stand. Maika walked back, not looking at Agathe, not looking at Aydan, and sat down with her hands folded.

They played her sixteen bars. The melody rose, wandered, called from its other room, and at bar fifteen the chord beneath it pulled, and the final C landed like a door finally closing on a quiet house. In the last row someone she could not see hummed the ending back, once, to themselves. Maika listened for whether they got the F.

activity: to read an ocean current map and explain how the Gulf Stream warms northern Europe
knowledge_domain: to read an ocean current map and explain how the Gulf Stream warms northern Europe
fact: London lies at about 51.5 degrees north, farther north than any point in the contiguous United States.
story:
The trail climbed out of the pines into open granite, and Mr. Chea called a rest at the overlook. Katherine sat on a flat rock and took the laminated current map out of the side pocket of her pack, spreading it over her knees so the wind couldn't take it. The paper was printed from the school library's database, all arrows and temperature gradients, the North Atlantic drawn like something alive.

"You brought homework up a mountain," Dax said, dropping beside her with his water bottle.

"It's not homework anymore. Presentation's Monday. I just don't have it yet."

Mr. Chea crouched at the edge of the overlook, pointing out to the group where the valley floor dropped toward a river they could hear but not see. Alma came over last, tying her hair back, and leaned in over Katherine's shoulder at the swirl of arrows crossing the ocean.

"So that's the Gulf Stream," Alma said. "It looks warm. All that red."

"It carries warm water north, and then east, toward Europe. That's the whole idea I have to explain." Katherine ran her finger along the current's path, up the coast of North America and then the long curve toward Ireland. "The problem is the map of Europe next to it. My scale's wrong. I kept assuming London sat around where New York is, and it doesn't."

Dax leaned over to look, chewing something. "Where is it?"

She rotated the regional map until the latitude lines ran straight, then laid her pen across the parallel that touched London. "London lies at about 51.5 degrees north. That's farther north than any point in the contiguous United States."

Dax stopped chewing. "No."

"Watch." She slid her pen left along the line, across the Atlantic, and let it come down on the coast of North America. It crossed the border. "The whole U.S.-Canada border along the forty-ninth parallel, basically. London's above that. Above all of it."

Alma laughed, one short note of genuine surprise. "So London is farther north than the border? Than the whole lower forty-eight?"

"Any point in the contiguous U.S.," Katherine said, and heard how precise it sounded, and didn't mind. "I spent two days on the wrong premise. I was building the whole talk around an Atlantic that was smaller than it is."

Mr. Chea had come over, quietly, the way he did, and stood with his hands in his jacket pockets reading the map over their heads without touching it. "What was the wrong premise?" he asked, which was how he asked everything, as if he genuinely wanted to know and would wait all day.

"That warmth needed explaining only in the far north. I kept thinking of Europe as basically our latitude plus a little. It isn't. So now I have to say two true things at once, and I'm not sure yet how they fit." She tapped the current, then the latitude line. "The water moves heat, that part I can show with the map. And London sits far enough north that you'd expect different weather than it gets. But I can't stand up there and pretend I understand every link between the two. Some of it I only know as lines on paper."

"That's not a weakness in a talk," Mr. Chea said. "That's the talk."

Dax was still squinting at the pen line on the border. "Can I tell people this? Like, tonight? 'London's farther north than all of the lower forty-eight.'"

"That's the one fact," Katherine said, "I actually have."

They shouldered their packs when Mr. Chea gave the word, and the trail bent back into the trees. Katherine folded the map but kept it in her hand instead of the pocket. She was composing the opening in her head, less cerebral than she'd planned, starting with Dax's face at the overlook instead of a diagram. She thought about how she'd tried to parametrize the whole climate system into one clean variable, one line of cause, and how the Atlantic had refused. Somewhere in her was still the itch of complicity with her own earlier shortcut, the comfortable map where London sat where she'd needed it to sit.

"You're smiling," Alma said, catching her stride.

"I'm going to open with a pen and a map and one sentence that made Dax stop eating." Katherine tucked the map into her jacket, against her chest where the wind wouldn't reach it. "Let's see if Mr. Chea lets me borrow his laser pointer."

activity: to debate whether an ancient religious rule still applies in modern life using the text itself
knowledge_domain: to debate whether an ancient religious rule still applies in modern life using the text itself
fact: The Mishnah, the first major written collection of Jewish oral law, was compiled around 200 CE under Rabbi Judah ha-Nasi.
story:
The festival had taken over the whole park by noon, booths of lacquered fans and dumplings and hand-lettered signs, and Colton stood in front of the one he'd been avoiding all summer: the synagogue's table, where Mr. Ito had taped up a question in marker on butcher paper. Does an ancient rule about rest still mean anything when your whole life runs on a phone? Below it, a stack of pamphlets and a sign-up sheet for a debate in September, two months away, in the library basement.

He hadn't meant to stop. He'd meant to find Felicity, who was working the Hawaiian shave ice booth and had promised him a free medium if he helped carry ice. But the question had a hook in it, because his grandmother kept Shabbat and his father didn't, and nobody in his family ever said why out loud. It just sat there between them like a border neither crossed.

"You're staring," Mr. Ito said. He was handing a pamphlet to a woman with a stroller, and he did it without hurry, the way he did everything.

"I'm not signing up," Colton said.

"I didn't ask you to." Mr. Ito turned back to the table. "But you're the third person today who's read it twice."

That was how it started, honestly, by accident and by pride. Colton signed the sheet to prove he could walk away from it, and then he had to actually do it, and doing it meant the thing Mr. Ito had written on the flyer: argue from the text itself. No feelings, no history-channel trivia, no quoting something a rabbi said on the internet. The Torah said keep the Sabbath and do no work, and that was where the trouble began, because when Colton sat at his desk that first night with a borrowed Tanakh open to Exodus, he found the strange, obvious problem: the Torah never listed what counted as work. It said don't do it. It didn't say what it was.

He texted Felicity, who was better at arguing than anyone he knew. "The rule bans something it never defines," he wrote. "How do you debate a rule like that? It's like a law against disturbance in a library that never says what noise is."

"Maybe the definition is somewhere else," she wrote back, and then, a minute later, "or maybe it was never supposed to be written down at all. Some rules are oral on purpose."

That idea wouldn't leave him alone. He went to the library the next morning and asked the reference librarian, who was no help, and then he did the thing he should have done first and asked Mr. Ito, who was unstacking chairs in the social hall. Mr. Ito didn't answer. He wrote a word on a scrap of paper and handed it over. Mishnah, it said, and underneath, one line: compiled around 200 CE under Rabbi Judah ha-Nasi. "That's not an answer," Mr. Ito said, before Colton could ask. "That's the door."

So Colton found out for himself, at a table near the windows while the boreal light of an August storm came down gray and level through the glass. The Mishnah was the first major written collection of Jewish oral law. Two thousand years ago, roughly, under a rabbi whose title meant the Prince, the whole accumulated conversation about what the Torah meant, all of it living in memory and argument, got set down at last. And there it was: the thirty-nine categories of work forbidden on Shabbat, worked out by generations of rabbis precisely because the Torah was silent, argued from clues in the text itself, from the words used for building the tabernacle. The rule had never been floating free. It had been held, all that time, in human hands.

He called Miller, who would be arguing the other side in September. "I found the answer to my own problem," Colton said, "and now I have a worse one."

"Those are the best kind," Miller said. "Tell me."

"The rule applies, that's my side, I can actually argue it now. The prohibition on work isn't vague, it's specified, in a document older than most countries. But here's the thing." He stared at the storm sliding across the parking lot. "The specification is human. Rabbis decided. Which means the rule was never just handed down complete. It was built. And if people built it, people can ask whether it still fits. So I can't stand up there and say the ancient rule applies because it's ancient. That's not even true. It applies because a lot of people spent a lot of centuries thinking hard about it, and I have to decide whether that thinking still holds." He paused. "I think it does. Rest as a boundary, as something you can't opt out of, because otherwise you will. That part feels true now, maybe truer now. But I can't prove it the way I can prove where the definition came from. That part I still have to hold open."

Miller was quiet for a second. "That's the most honest opening argument I've ever heard, and I'm going to destroy it."

"Good," Colton said. "Then I'll learn something twice."

At the festival's closing evening, after the lanterns were lit along the paths and the shave ice booth had sold out, Colton found his grandmother sitting on a folding chair near the stage, a paper plate of noodles balanced on her knee. He sat beside her. He hadn't planned what to say, so he said the truest available thing. "I've been studying Shabbat," he told her. "For a debate. The Mishnah and everything."

His grandmother looked at him for a long moment, and the lantern light moved across her face. "So my grandson learns a page," she said, and pushed the plate toward him. "Eat. Tell me what it says."

activity: volunteering at a community food bank for the first time
knowledge_domain: volunteering at a community food bank for the first time
fact: The US Bill Emerson Good Samaritan Food Donation Act of 1996 gives food donors limited protection from liability, which encourages stores and restaurants to donate surplus food.
story:
Isabelle arrived at the community garden at eight with a sun hat she borrowed from her mother and a form she had signed the night before. The plot behind the greenhouse had been given over to the food bank two summers ago, and most of the volunteers were older women who already knew which beds held the tomatoes. Ms. Quinn, who ran the distribution table, handed Isabelle a scale and a clipboard and told her to weigh everything that came in from the morning harvest.

Her want was simple and slightly embarrassing to her: forty service hours for her scholarship application, logged before September. She had picked the garden because it was close to her bus route, and because a girl on her floor, describing her own summer at a legal clinic, had called Isabelle a dilettante for choosing flowers and vegetables. Isabelle had not argued. She was not sure the word was wrong, and that bothered her more than the insult.

By ten, Lucius from her economics class had shown up with three crates of zucchini he had wheeled over on a skateboard. "Surplus," he said, nonchalant, tipping the crates onto the scale. "My uncle overplanted." Isabelle recorded eleven pounds and watched Ms. Quinn price the crates for the afternoon distribution, and it occurred to her that she had never thought about how free food acquires a cost, how someone decides what a pound of zucchini is worth to a family that cannot pay for it.

The bread arrived at noon. A car pulled up to the gate and a woman began carrying out paper bags full of loaves, still smelling of the ovens at the bakery she owned. Isabelle went to help her and noticed the woman hesitating at the tailgate, one bag held against her hip.

"You can put those on the table under the canopy," Isabelle said.

"I know, I've done this before," the woman said, and then, quieter, "Last week I almost didn't come. My partner worries someone gets sick and sues us." She set the bag down. "Then I tell him about the Bill Emerson Good Samaritan Food Donation Act of 1996. Food donors get limited protection from liability. That's why stores and restaurants like us donate surplus food at all." She smiled at the loaves as if they had settled the argument themselves.

Lucius had come over to carry the second load, and on the walk back to the canopy he said, "So the law basically indemnifies her. Partially." Isabelle said she didn't think it worked like an insurance policy, exactly, and Lucius shrugged and said protection was protection, and they dropped the subject because Ms. Quinn was calling for help sorting the bruised tomatoes from the whole ones.

That afternoon Ms. Quinn sat down beside Isabelle on the overturned crate that served as a bench, and it was her view that filled the next hour. She had watched the garden change hands twice, and she had learned to read a volunteer's face the way she read the sky before deciding to water. This one, the girl with the clipboard, was counting hours, but she was also counting something else, something in the way she wrote down each family's name without being asked twice. Ms. Quinn remembered being eighteen and believing that generosity was a fixed quantity, something you either had or performed, and she had needed thirty years to learn it was more like a garden bed, something you improved or let go weedy depending on the season.

"Can I ask you something?" Isabelle said. "The bread lady. If the law protects her, why was she still scared?"

"Because the law is one thing and a lawsuit is another thing," Ms. Quinn said. "You can be protected and still be frightened. Look at half the people who come to this table." She picked up a zucchini from Lucius's crates and turned it in her hand.

Isabelle remembered, then, the autumn her father's restaurant had closed. She was eleven. At the end there had been a walk-in cooler full of food and a landlord with a padlock, and her father had stood in the alley for a long time before letting most of it spoil, because he could not afford, that month, to be wrong about what he was allowed to give away. She had not thought of the alley in years, and she had never once connected it to a bakery owner's fear at a tailgate.

She filled in the last line of her log sheet, but she kept thinking about Lucius calling the law indemnity and the bakery owner calling it protection, and how the same words sat differently in their mouths. She was going to look up the act when she got home, the actual text, not a summary, and she was going to email her father a question she had never thought to ask him. For now she stood up, brushed the soil from her knees, and carried the crate of tomatoes toward the line of people already forming at the gate.

activity: to trace the steps of cellular respiration from glucose to ATP in the mitochondria
knowledge_domain: to trace the steps of cellular respiration from glucose to ATP in the mitochondria
fact: When muscle cells run low on oxygen, they convert pyruvate into lactate, which regenerates NAD+ so glycolysis can continue making 2 ATP per glucose.
story:
The trail behind the reservoir had one bench, one sign about poison ivy, and, as far as Vincent could tell, no mitochondria, which was a problem, because his biology exam was Monday and his mother had ordered him out of the house on the grounds that he had been sitting at his desk since breakfast making a small somatic monument of despair, shoulders curved like parentheses. He brought the flashcards anyway. Twenty-six of them, rubber-banded, covering cellular respiration from glucose to ATP, and he had read the first card so many times that the words had begun to lose meaning, glycolysis dissolving into a sound a sick animal might make.

Johnathan and Sahil met him at the trailhead because they had nothing better to do and because Sahil, at least, claimed that walking improved memory. Johnathan claimed that walking improved nothing and that he came for the company, which he expressed by taking the flashcards out of Vincent's hand and reading them aloud in the voice of a sports announcer.

"Glucose enters the cell, ladies and gentlemen, and is split in the cytoplasm."

"Give those back."

"It's a ten-step process. The crowd is on its feet."

They walked. The trail ran along the water and then cut inland through a field of tall grass, mown at the edges, wild in the middle, belonging, according to a sagging fence, to Mr. Wang, who was convalescing on his porch after a knee operation and who watched teenagers cross the corner of his field with a tolerance that had limits neither of them had ever tested successfully. Vincent kept trying to recite the cards in order. Glycolysis in the cytoplasm, then pyruvate, then the Krebs cycle, then the electron transport chain in the mitochondria, where most of the ATP got made. He could hold the sequence for about forty seconds before it collapsed, and he had begun to suspect that memorizing it flat, like a phone number, was the wrong approach, though he could not yet say what the right one was.

"Race you to the fence," Johnathan said, in the middle of the field, for no reason Vincent could determine other than that the fence was there and Johnathan was bored. "Winner gets the flashcards burned."

"That's my property being wagered."

"Winner gets to not have the flashcards burned."

Vincent ran. He was not a runner, but he was seventeen and the grass was flat and for the first thirty seconds it felt like flight. Then his thighs began to burn, a heat that climbed from deep in the muscle, and his legs turned to something heavier than legs, and Johnathan pulled ahead and touched the fence post while Vincent stopped with his hands on his knees, breathing like a landed fish, the whole grand pageant of his study plan reduced in one field to a boy drooling slightly onto Mr. Wang's grass. There was a kind of bathos in it that even he could appreciate, once he could breathe.

"It's lactate," Sahil said, catching up at an unhurried jog. Sahil ran cross-country and had opinions about legs.

"What is?"

"The burn. When your muscle cells run low on oxygen, they convert pyruvate into lactate. That's what it's called. Lactate."

Vincent, still bent over, looked up at him. "That's on my cards. That's card nineteen."

"It regenerates NAD-plus," Sahil said, with a shrug that suggested he was quoting his coach and did not much care whether the terms were right. "So glycolysis can keep going. Two ATP per glucose. It's not much but it's something."

Vincent straightened up slowly. Something assembled itself in his head, the way the field assembled itself when you stopped running and the world stopped sliding. The cards were a sequence, a phone number, but here was the same material arranged as a thing that had just happened inside his legs. His cells had been short of oxygen, and instead of shutting down they had done this crude, minimal thing, pyruvate to lactate, NAD-plus back, glycolysis limping along at two ATP per glucose, a backup generator in a storm. It was inefficient and it was why he could still move at all. The fact on card nineteen was not a fact about diagrams. It was a fact about the inside of his own thighs, which were still trembling in a personal, insulted way.

"I think I've been studying it backwards," he said. "I've been trying to memorize the map. But it's more like, the map is what your body does when you sprint through a field."

"That's beautiful," Johnathan said. "Can we burn the cards now?"

"No. I need them." Vincent fished them out of his pocket, and the rubber band snapped, and twenty-six cards sprayed into the grass, glycolysis face-down in a cow pie. He stood looking at them, and Sahil began to laugh, and somewhere behind them Mr. Wang rose from his porch and started down his steps toward the fence, unhurried, leaning on a cane, in no doubt at all about whose field had just been littered.

"Pick them up," Mr. Wang called. "All of them."

activity: to compare two apartment leases and work out the total monthly cost including utilities
knowledge_domain: to compare two apartment leases and work out the total monthly cost including utilities
fact: Some leases require the tenant to carry renter's insurance, which covers the tenant's own belongings rather than the building and adds a monthly premium.
story:
The two leases lay side by side on the kitchen table, and Kate had read the second one three times before she noticed the sentence. It sat between a clause about pest control and a clause about quiet hours, unremarkable as a seam: tenant shall carry renter's insurance. She read it aloud to the empty kitchen, then once more silently, as though a slower reading might dissolve it.

"Problem?" Averie was at the counter making tea, the kettle ticking as it cooled. She and Meriem had come over to help, though so far their help had consisted mostly of eating the popcorn Kate had made and arguing about whether the apartment on Halden Street had better light.

"There's a line in here about insurance," Kate said. "Renter's insurance."

"That's a thing?" Meriem pulled her chair around and leaned over Kate's shoulder, her braid falling into the scatter of papers. "I thought that was for, like, landlords. Buildings."

"Renters insurance covers your stuff, though. Not the building. Yours. Your own belongings." Kate tapped the sentence with one finger. "But it costs money. Every month. It's a premium. And this lease says I have to carry it."

Averie set her mug down. "So the Halden place isn't as cheap as you thought."

Kate laid her palm flat over the Bellamy lease, the cheaper one, the one she had been quietly favoring for a week. The rent was forty dollars less than Halden, which had seemed decisive until now. She pulled a fresh sheet of paper toward her and drew a line down the middle, the way her father did when he balanced the checkbook, and the smallness of the gesture made her throat tighten. She wrote Halden on the left and Bellamy on the right and started listing numbers beneath each: rent, the water and trash fee both buildings charged, the internet she'd have to buy either way. Then, on the right only, she wrote insurance and left a blank.

"How much is a premium?" Meriem asked.

"I don't know yet. That's the problem. If it's ten dollars, Bellamy still wins. If it's forty, they're the same. If it's more than that..." She let the sentence go unfinished, the way you do when finishing it would make it real.

Ms. Flores from next door had let herself in through the back door, as she did on Sunday afternoons, carrying a foil pan of rice she always claimed was too much for one person. She set it on the stove and peered at the table over the rim of her glasses. "Apartments," she said. "You're all leaving, then."

"Kate's leaving," Averie said. "We're just eating her popcorn."

"Renters insurance," Ms. Flores read, in her unhurried way. "I've had a policy since I was twenty-two. Covers my own belongings if something happens, not the building. The landlord's insurance handles the building." She lifted the foil off the rice and stirred it, and the steam carried up a smell of cumin. "Not expensive, in my experience. But it's every month. It adds up like anything else adds up."

Kate wrote a small note in the margin, then made herself a plate of rice even though she wasn't hungry, because refusing would have been an argument, and Ms. Flores ruled her kitchen visits like a small benevolent autocrat, immune to the word no. "Did you comparison shop yours?" Kate asked. "When you started?"

"I asked at the same place that does my car insurance, and I took the first number they gave me. Don't do that." Ms. Flores said it with a sardonic lift of her eyebrow, aimed, apparently, at her younger self.

By six o'clock Kate had quotes. She'd called two companies while Meriem washed the popcorn bowl and Averie dried, and the numbers were close together, close enough that she used the larger one to be safe. She wrote it in the blank on her chart and added each column twice, checking her arithmetic the way she checked exam answers, alert for the small treachery of carrying a wrong digit. Bellamy came out ahead by eleven dollars. Eleven dollars, once the insurance premium was counted in, and only because Bellamy's water fee was lower.

"Eleven dollars," Meriem said, reading over her shoulder. "That's, what, two coffees."

"It's eleven dollars every month for a year," Kate said. "A hundred and thirty-two dollars." But that wasn't the whole of it, and she knew it. Halden had a dishwasher and a window over the sink, and it was four blocks closer to campus, and in February, when the wind came off the river, four blocks mattered. Bellamy was on the bus line, which meant a pass, which meant another number she hadn't written down yet. She reached for the pen again.

"Stop," Averie said, gently. "You're going to be doing this all night."

"There's a bus pass."

"There's walking. You have legs."

Kate looked at the chart, at the two columns with their ragged unequal lengths, and understood something she couldn't yet say in a sentence: that the comparison wasn't really about money, it was about what she was willing to trade, and no arithmetic could decide that for her. The numbers could narrow the question but not close it. Eleven dollars said Bellamy. The window over the sink said Halden. The insurance said Bellamy by less each month than she'd feared, which was its own kind of relief, though the relief arrived tempered by the knowledge that she'd nearly signed the lease without reading that far.

She folded the chart in half and put it in her back pocket. "I'm going to look at Halden again tomorrow," she said. "In the morning. I want to see the light in that kitchen before I decide."

"Forestall all you want," Meriem said. "You're choosing the window."

Kate laughed, and didn't answer, and carried the plates to the sink while the last of the daylight moved across the table and the two leases lay where she'd left them, side by side, still unresolved.

activity: how interest makes borrowed money cost more over time and makes savings grow
knowledge_domain: how interest makes borrowed money cost more over time and makes savings grow
fact: APY, annual percentage yield, includes the effect of compounding, so a savings rate of 4.65 percent compounded monthly is quoted as 4.75 percent APY.
story:
The poster in the credit union window had two numbers on it, and Benjamin stood outside for a long moment trying to decide which one was a lie. He had walked here with ninety-one dollars folded in his sock, which was not his money in any sense he could defend, and he had told himself on the way over that he was here to open a savings account, which was also not exactly true.

Inside, the lobby smelled like carpet cleaner and toner. A smaller version of the same poster hung above the desk where a man in a gray vest, his name tag reading Mr. Nowak, was helping an older woman count something into a tube. Benjamin took a brochure and read it again, as if the fluorescent lighting might change the arithmetic. Savings rate, 4.65 percent, compounded monthly. Then, underneath, in bolder type: 4.75 percent APY. He had done all right in precalculus. He understood that one of these numbers described the other, that the bigger one was what the smaller one turned into, but he could not have said why a bank would advertise both, unless it was the same reason a menu printed the weight of the steak before cooking.

"You're blocking the brochure rack," Madyson said behind him. She worked Saturdays at the pharmacy two doors down and had crossed the street still wearing her name tag, which said TRAINING. "Also you've been staring at that thing like it owes you money."

"It kind of does," Benjamin said. He tapped the smaller number. "Four point six five. But the big one says four point seven five APY. Same account. Why is it two numbers?"

"APY includes the effect of compounding," she said, in the flat voice she used when quoting something she'd read on a break. "So the rate and the yield aren't the same thing. Or something. They make you memorize it in training." She picked at her name tag. "Why are you actually here? You told Rowen you were going to the lake."

He hadn't told Rowen that. He had told Rowen he was going to the credit union, and Rowen had said he was going to the lake, and somewhere between Saturday morning and now the two plans had merged into a version where Benjamin was a liar, which was convenient, because it saved everyone the trouble of what he was actually doing. He looked at the tube of money under Mr. Nowak's fingers and thought about his father's tool chest, the latch he had snapped in the parking lot of the hardware store while loading it, and the forty dollars of his own he had already put back, and the ninety-one he had earned at the pharmacy by taking Madyson's uncovered shifts, which meant it was his money, technically, except that he had let her believe he was saving it for a car stereo so she would not ask about the tool chest, which made it feel borrowed.

"Restitution," he said.

"What?"

"Nothing. A word from Mr. Nowak's class." This was also not true; the word had come to him in the parking lot three weeks ago, kneeling over the broken latch, and he had liked it because it sounded cleaner than guilt, like something you could pay and walk away from. "I want to open a savings account. And I have a question about a loan."

Mr. Nowak finished with the older woman and waved Benjamin up. Up close his eyes had a jaundiced cast, yellowed at the edges, and his hands moved over the keyboard without looking. "Savings first?" He slid a form across. "Rate's competitive right now. You saw the poster."

"Which number is the real one?" Benjamin asked. He put the ninety-one dollars on the counter, and Madyson, standing beside him, looked at the money and then at him with an expression he would think about later, at the counter and on the walk home and probably after that.

"They both are," Mr. Nowak said. "Four sixty-five is the rate, compounded monthly. The APY, four seventy-five, is what that works out to over a year with the compounding folded in. It's the honest number, if anything. Some places quote the rate big and the yield small." He keyed something in. "Loan question?"

"Personal loan. Small. For repairs."

"Collateral? Cosigner?" Mr. Nowak turned the monitor toward him. "Because interest runs the other direction, you understand. A loan at a rate like that costs you more every month you carry it. The same compounding that grows your savings grows what you owe. People forget that half."

Benjamin looked at the form in front of him, the line for the deposit amount, and understood that he did not need a loan at all, that the ninety-one dollars in his sock was already the restitution, and that the loan had been a way of keeping his father in the story as someone who could still be surprised by his son's honesty, rather than someone who had quietly replaced the latch weeks ago and said nothing, which was what Madyson was now, in a low voice, telling him.

"He bought a new one at the store," she said. "I rang it up. He said, don't tell Ben, he'll try to pay me back."

Mr. Nowak waited with his pen, patient as a man who watched people bring money in and carry it out all day and had long ago decided it was not his business which direction the arithmetic went. Benjamin picked up the pen and held it over the deposit line. He could put the money in the account with the two numbers, let it compound, let the smaller one become the larger one, and give his father something other than cash at Christmas. Or he could walk home with it and put it in the tool chest, where it would sit in the dark, earning nothing, cauterizing a debt that had apparently already been forgiven without his permission.
