"That account," he said to Mr. Nowak. "The four point seven five. Does it have to stay in for the whole year to count?"

"It counts either way," Mr. Nowak said. "The year is just how it's measured."

Benjamin wrote the number ninety-one on the line, then sat back and looked at the poster through the lobby glass, at the two percentages side by side, and thought about which one he was.

"Deposit it," Madyson said. "Then we'll go find Rowen, and you can lie to him about the lake."

activity: to interview for a part-time job with confident eye contact and clear answers
knowledge_domain: to interview for a part-time job with confident eye contact and clear answers
fact: Albert Mehrabian's often-quoted '7 percent words, 38 percent tone, 55 percent face' rule came from experiments on conveying feelings, and he said it does not apply to all communication.
story:
The flyer had been taped to the door of the student services office since September, and Paige had walked past it twice a day without stopping, until the Thursday her mother's hours at the clinic got cut and the walk home turned into a long arithmetic problem. The Book Nook on Marsh Street wanted a weekend clerk, interviews Friday at four, and the flyer asked applicants to be prepared to discuss customer service. Paige took a photo of it with her phone, then stood in the hallway feeling the photo change from evidence into an obligation.

By lunch she had a plan, or rather Denzel had one for her. He slid his phone across the cafeteria table with a video paused at the thirty-second mark. "Watch this. It changes everything." The video said that only seven percent of communication was words. Thirty-eight percent was tone. Fifty-five percent was your face. "So basically," Denzel said, leaning back with the satisfaction of someone delivering a verdict, "your answers don't matter. You could say you hate books. Just look like you love them."

Paige watched the video twice, and something in her loosened. She had spent years constructing sentences carefully and watching them land nowhere, and here was proof that the sentences had been a kind of decoration, that everyone had really been reading her face all along. That night she practiced in the bathroom mirror, arranging her eyebrows, her mouth, softening her chin. She said nothing at all for the first ten minutes, just held an expression of warm competence, and it felt less like rehearsal than like assembling a costume. There was a small unease under it, the way a word on the tip of the tongue is both present and unreachable, but she set the unease aside. The interview was in sixteen hours.

On Friday morning, Ashton found her in the library copying interview questions onto index cards, though the cards were blank on the answer side. "You didn't write anything down?" Paige told her about the percentages, quickly, like sharing a secret. Ashton frowned at the cards. "That seems too easy." Paige was already defensive, already hearing her own certainty as a performance. "It's from experiments," she said. "It's science." But the word experiments caught in her mind afterward, a splinter she couldn't stop pressing. Experiments about what, exactly?

The library had one computer that wasn't blocked for updates, and it was free because the period before lunch was when everyone else commodified their free time into the vending machines. Paige searched the researcher's name, Mehrabian, and found the trail of what he had actually said. The numbers were real, the seven, the thirty-eight, the fifty-five, but they came out of experiments about conveying feelings, feelings only, and Mehrabian himself had said the rule did not apply to all communication. She read the sentence three times. She thought about the Book Nook manager asking her how she would handle a refund for a damaged book, and she understood, with a sinking and clarifying feeling at once, that a refund procedure was not a feeling. Her face could not process a return.

She found Ms. Farah-Ali in the English office during the last period and stood in the doorway holding her blank index cards like a confession. "I thought the words didn't matter," Paige said, "because of a statistic, but it only counts for feelings. He said so himself. He said it doesn't apply to all communication." Ms. Farah-Ali looked up from a stack of essays, and Paige braced for the lecture, the lugubrious speech about the internet and critical thinking that teachers seemed to keep folded in their pockets. Instead Ms. Farah-Ali asked one question. "So what do you actually want to say tomorrow?" And Paige, who had spent a day and a half working on her face, opened her mouth and found she had no answer prepared, and that this was the real thing she had to fix before four o'clock.

She sat in the empty office while Ms. Farah-Ali graded, and she wrote. She wrote that she had reorganized her aunt's garage last summer and had made a system anyone could follow after she left, which was, she realized, what a store was. She wrote that when a customer at her mother's clinic complained about a billing error, Paige had been the one who stayed calm, though she privately suspected her calm had been useless and the resolution had come from the words the receptionist used. That was the part she couldn't reconcile. Maybe her face had mattered in that moment and maybe it hadn't. She thought of the courtroom shows her father watched, how an acquittal could turn on a lawyer's steady voice or on a single phrase that happened to fit the truth, and how no one could ever say afterward which one had done it. She wrote in the margin of the card: both, probably, in ways nobody can measure. It wasn't a satisfying answer. She underlined it anyway.

At three forty-five she stood outside the Book Nook in the shirt she had ironed while rehearsing her opening line, and through the window she could see a woman at the register explaining something to a teenager in a green apron, pointing at a screen, the teenager nodding. Paige checked her reflection in the glass, saw the face she had practiced, and decided to let it do its work but not to depend on it. She had her cards in her back pocket, and on the top card, in her own handwriting, was the first true sentence she had prepared in two days.

She pushed the door open, and a bell rang above her, and the woman at the register said, "You must be the four o'clock. Come on in."

activity: how rent, mortgages, deposits and down payments work when someone pays for a place to live
knowledge_domain: how rent, mortgages, deposits and down payments work when someone pays for a place to live
fact: The word 'mortgage' comes from Old French for 'dead pledge', because the pledge ends either when the debt is paid or when the property is forfeited.
story:
The envelope had been sitting by the toaster since Tuesday, and Grace's grandmother had not opened it, which was how Grace knew it was from the landlord. She watched her grandmother pour coffee with the careful deliberation of someone negotiating an armistice with the morning, then slid the envelope across the kitchen table and slit it with a butter knife before she could decide not to. The rent was going up two hundred dollars a month. The deposit, the letter said, would carry over, which her grandmother read aloud twice, as though repetition might change what it meant.

"So the deposit moves with us," Grace said. "Like it's ours, but they hold it."

"Like a hostage," her grandmother said. "Money you give them to prove you'll behave. You get it back when you leave, if the walls are clean and the stove isn't ruined." She set down her cup. Grace noticed her thumb moving along the rim, once around, twice, the way she did when she was doing sums she didn't want to say out loud.

Grace had been saving since September, babysitting and weekends at the garden center, and there was a little over four thousand dollars in the account, which until this morning she had thought of as college money. She said nothing about it. Instead she pulled out her phone, because Tyrone's family had bought a house last spring and he had complained about the process for months, and he was awake at eleven on a Saturday, always. He texted back fast: the down payment had been the hard part, tens of thousands, cash you hand the bank up front so they trust you with the rest. His parents had borrowed from his grandmother too. Then, before Grace could answer: also they made his parents prove they could afford it forever, pay stubs, everything.

On her screen was a listing for a small house eight blocks away, and beside the price was a monthly number smaller than her grandmother's new rent. That couldn't be right. She tapped it and found a calculator, and when she put in a down payment of twenty thousand the payment barely moved, and when she put in five thousand it jumped. The bank lent most of the money and you paid it back over thirty years, the site said, plus interest, which the site did not want to talk about at length. The word for the loan was mortgage, and there, in a footnote, was the part that made Grace put the phone flat on the table.

"Grandma. Why is it called that?"

"Called what?"

"Mortgage. It's from Old French. It means dead pledge. Dead pledge. That's actually where the word comes from." She turned the screen around. Her grandmother leaned in, squinting, and then sat back and laughed, a short, surprised sound.

"Dead pledge," she repeated. "That's very honest of them."

Grace read on, because the footnote went further, the way footnotes do when they've decided to tell you something. The pledge ended when the debt was paid, or when the property was forfeit. It died at the finish line or it died in the ditch, and either way it was over, and the word had been carrying that around for centuries while people said it cheerfully at dinner parties. She tried to imagine her uncle Phil, who was irascible about almost nothing except money, saying the phrase at a barbecue, oblivious.

Manreet texted a photo from the college visit her parents had dragged her on, a dorm room the size of a closet, and beneath it: this costs HOW much per year. Grace looked from the phone to the listing to her grandmother, who had taken out a pad of paper and was writing numbers down the margin, and something in her felt like two rooms whose doors had opened onto the same hallway. The money could be a down payment someday, or it could be tuition, and the second one was a pledge too, one that would end when she graduated or when she couldn't pay, and she had never once thought of it that way. She didn't know which use made the money more hers. Maybe owning a house enfranchised you in a way renting never did, a vote in your own life, Tyrone's mother said so constantly. But her grandmother had rented for forty years and was the most settled person Grace knew.

"I could put some toward it," Grace said, and heard her own voice arrive before her plan did. "Not all of it. Some."

Her grandmother stopped writing. Outside, a neighbor's dog began its morning argument with a squirrel, and the refrigerator hummed its single note, and her grandmother looked at her over the pad of paper for a long moment, pen still in hand.

"First you eat your eggs," she said, and slid the pan from the stove.

activity: to use a geographic information system to overlay flood risk and housing on a city map
knowledge_domain: to use a geographic information system to overlay flood risk and housing on a city map
fact: In 1854, physician John Snow mapped cholera deaths in London and showed they clustered around one water pump on Broad Street, an early example of spatial analysis.
story:
Dylan had claimed the computer by the window in the public library for two hours straight, and the librarian had begun to orbit him like a suspicious moon. On the screen, the city floated in layers: streets, then a wash of blue where the river might rise, then small squares for houses. His assignment, self-assigned and therefore nonnegotiable, was to overlay flood risk and housing and find out who lived in the blue.

"Are you going to eat that granola bar or commune with it?" Eliam dropped into the chair beside him, spinning it once.

"I'm interpolating," Dylan said, with enormous dignity. The software was filling in the blank spaces between the river's measured elevations, guessing, in its tidy mathematical way, how far the water would creep. "Between known points. It's guessing, basically. Polite guessing."

"You've been polite-guessing since four o'clock."

Alma arrived with a stack of printouts and the expression of someone carrying news. She dealt the papers onto the desk like cards. "Your introduction," she said. "Mr. Francis said you can't just start with 'maps are cool.'"

"Maps are cool."

"He was fairly trenchant about it. He said the whole first paragraph has to go, and also that you spelled 'neighborhood' wrong twice in two different ways, which he described as a talent."

Dylan scrolled his draft, wounded. The introduction needed an example, something old and famous, and he'd been circling it all afternoon like a word on the tip of his tongue. Then he found it, or nearly found it, in one of Alma's printouts, a mention of an old physician. He typed the name and leaned back. "Okay. In 1854, this doctor, John Snow, mapped cholera deaths in London. Showed they clustered around one water pump. Broad Street." He pointed at the sentence as if presenting a jury with Exhibit A. "That's spatial analysis. Before computers. Before, like, electricity in homes."

"So he put deaths on a map," Eliam said, "and the map said the pump."

"The map said the pump." Dylan felt the click of it, the old story and his blue wash of a city slotting together. One man, one map, dots crowding around a pump; him, one laptop, houses crowding into flood zones. Same idea, different century. He moved his mouse and stacked the housing layer over the flood layer, and the map answered him, though not in the way he'd hoped.

Alma saw it first. She'd gone quiet in a way that wasn't like her, and when Dylan followed her finger he understood why. The densest cluster of houses in the high-risk blue was the stretch of Martindale Road, the row of narrow porches where Eliam lived, where Eliam's grandmother kept a figurine collection on the sill and yelled at pigeons from the doorstep.

"Run it again," Eliam said. "You polite-guessed wrong. Interpolate harder."

Dylan ran it again with the higher-resolution elevation file Alma had found, and the blue crept, if anything, slightly closer. The houses stayed put. Houses always stay put; that, Dylan was beginning to understand, was the entire problem with houses, and with grandmothers, and with the way a city lays itself down along a river because rivers used to be convenient.

"I'm going to tell her we need renters insurance," Eliam said, in the voice of someone rehearsing. "She's going to say the river has never once come up the porch in sixty years, and she'll be right, and also it's not about the last sixty years, is it."

"That's actually a decent line for your conclusion," Alma said. "You can have it. I'm feeling generous."

Mr. Francis passed behind them on his way to the periodicals, paused, squinted at the screen, and said only, "Better paragraph two," which from him was a parade.

Later, when the library lights dimmed for closing and Eliam had gone to walk his news home, Dylan sat with the map still glowing and did not close it. He thought about John Snow, dots around a pump, and how a map could tell you where the trouble was and still not tell you what to do about it. He couldn't say what the city would decide, or whether anyone with power would even look, or whether the polite guesses had been polite enough. He saved the file twice, then a third time to a drive in his pocket.

"Sir, we're closing," the librarian said, hovering with her ring of keys.

"One second." He zoomed in once more on Martindale Road, counted the porches, and printed the map.

activity: to write a research paper with an argument, footnotes and a bibliography in a standard citation style
knowledge_domain: to write a research paper with an argument, footnotes and a bibliography in a standard citation style
fact: The Chicago Manual of Style, whose notes-and-bibliography system uses footnotes, was first published by the University of Chicago Press in 1906.
story:
The laptop had four hours of battery left and no charger, because Cameron had left the charger in his mother's car, and his mother was already two hours toward home. That was the arithmetic he did on the porch of his grandfather's house while the screen dimmed itself to fifteen percent and the assignment sheet sat open in his email: eight pages, an argument, footnotes, a bibliography in a proper citation style, due Monday at eight in the morning. It was Friday night. The house had one computer, in the den, a squat machine his grandfather used for email and for a game of solitaire whose cards Cameron had never once seen him lose.

He had never written anything with footnotes. At school the teachers had wanted, variously, "claims," "evidence," "analysis," words that slid off him like rain off wax. His thesis, at the moment, was that the interstate highway system had destroyed American cities, which was a position he had borrowed whole from a documentary and could not have defended against a skeptical duck. Paityn, texting from her house across town, had already poked at it. "destroyed how," she wrote. "for whom. pick something you can prove." She was halfway through her own paper on the same deadline, which meant she had no time for him and gave it anyway.

The grandfather's den smelled of pipe smoke that had outlived the pipe. Cameron sat down at the old machine and found, stacked beside the monitor, a shelf of books he had walked past every summer of his life: almanacs, a dictionary with a cracked spine, and a thick orange volume, cloth-bound, its title in faded gilt. He pulled it out to look important on the desk, the way a person arranges props before a performance, and that was when Samara called.

"You're doing Chicago style, right?" she said. Samara was in his history class and had opinions about everything, including citation. "Sato assigned it specifically. Footnotes, not parentheticals. Everyone's complaining like it's a punishment invented to ruin our weekend." There was the sound of her laughing at someone off the phone. "Paityn made me look it up. The Chicago Manual of Style, the notes-and-bibliography system with the footnotes, the University of Chicago Press first published it in 1906. It's older than her great-grandparents. So it's not exactly a new torment designed for us."

"It's older than the highways," Cameron said, mostly to himself, and Samara said something about that being a weird way to put it, and then she was gone. He turned the orange book over in his hands. It was a later edition, but old, its corners soft with handling, and inside the front cover, in his grandfather's small upright hand, was a date from before Cameron's parents were born and a line of writing that made him sit very still: Property of the University of Chicago Library, withdrawn, sold, and beneath that, in different ink, a price his grandfather had paid at some sale Cameron knew nothing about.

He had assumed, his whole life, that his grandfather had been a machinist, because that was what everyone said at Thanksgiving, and because his hands were the kind that made the story credible. Cameron carried the book to the kitchen, where the old man was fixing a sandwich, and set it on the counter without a speech prepared, which was unlike him. "Where did you get this?" His grandfather dried his hands on the towel, looked at the cover, and then looked at Cameron for a long moment, long enough that the clock over the stove ticked through it twice.

"I wrote a thesis," his grandfather said finally. "A long time ago. Didn't finish it." He took the sandwich plate to the table but didn't sit. "Machinist paid for the first two years. Then your grandmother, she was pregnant with your mother, and I took the job at the plant and the library wanted its book back and I bought it instead at the sale because I couldn't stand to give it up entirely. Footnotes and all." He laughed, a short sound with something under it. "Three hundred pages on municipal water systems, if you can believe that. I still know how it would have ended."

Cameron did believe it, suddenly, the way you believe a door has been standing open in a house you thought you knew. He carried the Manual back to the den and opened it on the desk beside the humming computer, and instead of searching the internet for shortcuts, he worked through the notes-and-bibliography system the slow way, because the book was in his hands and because his grandfather's failing margin note on page after page said the same thing, a penciled injunction in the same small upright hand: Check the primary source. Always check the primary source.

So Cameron checked. He found the interstate argument falling apart in his hands, the way borrowed things do: the documentary had flattened sixty years into one cause, and the primary sources in his grandfather's almanacs and the county records he could reach before the battery died showed highways that had revived some towns and hollowed others, depending on decisions made later, by councils and banks, in rooms far from the blueprints. By two in the morning he had a new thesis, narrower and stranger and his own: that the highways were the instrument and not the hand. He could prove some of it. The rest stayed honestly uncertain, and he wrote a paragraph saying so, footnoted to two sources that disagreed with each other, which felt, for the first time, like a move and not a confession.

At sunrise he printed the draft on the old machine's wheezing printer, and his grandfather stood in the doorway with two cups of coffee, reading over Cameron's shoulder at the first footnote, the little superscript number like a raised hand at the back of a classroom. "Number one," the old man said. "Chicago." Cameron slid the orange volume across the desk, and his grandfather sat down and reached for a pencil.

activity: how unions, collective bargaining and labour laws shape wages, hours and working conditions
knowledge_domain: how unions, collective bargaining and labour laws shape wages, hours and working conditions
fact: Canada's Rand formula, from Justice Ivan Rand's 1946 ruling after a Ford strike in Windsor, Ontario, requires all workers covered by a union contract to pay dues.
story:
Alex counted the lines on his pay stub twice before folding it into his back pocket, and either way the arithmetic was the same: three hours of his wages had gone somewhere he had never agreed to go. He had been bagging groceries at Kessler's for five weeks, hired the week after his seventeenth birthday, and nobody at the orientation had mentioned a union, though the break room corkboard had held a faded notice about something called Local 229 the whole time. He asked Jeffrey about it during the Sunday close, sliding carts across the lot in the last orange light. Jeffrey, who had been there a year and treated the store's mysteries with the calm of a man who had survived worse, only shrugged and said everybody pays, that it comes off whether you join or not, and that complaining to the manager was a good way to get the worst shifts forever.

The manager, a small man named Mr. Nowak who wore a tie even on Saturdays, was not the ogre Alex had pictured. When Alex brought the stub to the office and asked, carefully, trying to propitiate him with a tone that suggested curiosity rather than grievance, why money was leaving his cheque for an organization he had never signed anything for, Mr. Nowak leaned back and looked almost pleased. "You noticed," he said. "Most of them never notice." He pulled a binder from the shelf behind him, blew dust off it, and slid it across the desk. It was a collective agreement, thick as a hymnal, its cover anachronistic in its plainness, and Mr. Nowak tapped a clause about wage scales and another about scheduling notice. "You work under this," he said. "Every person in this store does. Dues are part of it. Look up the Rand formula if you want the why of it. It's older than me." He did not explain further, which Alex found both infuriating and, somehow, respectful.

That night Alex sat at the kitchen table with his laptop while his mother watched something with the volume low. He found it faster than he expected. The Rand formula came out of Justice Ivan Rand's ruling in 1946, after a Ford strike in Windsor, Ontario, and it meant all workers covered by a union contract pay dues. Not just members. Everyone covered. He read the sentence three times, testing it against his own stub, and then read the local's page, which mentioned a grievance procedure, a safety committee, and a starting wage that was, he now realized, two dollars an hour above what the supermarket across the highway paid. He had taken that wage for granted, the way you take a floor for granted, and it unsettled him to learn there had been a floor built under him before he arrived.

The withheld thing came out on Wednesday. Margot, who worked the till and was in two of his classes, cornered him by the dairy cooler and told him the company was talking about a furlough for the students over the slow weeks in February, and that Mr. Nowak had said nothing to anyone because nothing was certain yet. "But there's a clause," she said, gripping a carton of cream like evidence. "There's a clause about layoffs. I looked. There's an order to it, seniority, notice. They can't just send us home because it's February." Alex understood, slowly, that the binder in the office was not paperwork about dues. It was the reason a furlough could not simply happen to them, and also the reason three hours of his money was gone.

The meeting was Thursday night in the union hall above the laundromat, and it was Mr. Nowak's perspective that mattered there, though Alex did not know it yet. Nowak had managed grocery stores for thirty years and had learned to hold two loyalties at once, the company's and his own conscience's, and lately the company's had been winning. He sat at the back while the local's rep, a woman with a hoarse voice, laid out the February numbers and asked for a show of hands on filing a grievance if the furlough went through without notice. Nowak raised his hand with the rest, and hated how surprised he was at himself, and watched the kid from the office, the one who'd counted his dues like a wrong, standing at the side taking it in.

Afterward Alex caught him in the stairwell, where the smell of detergent rose from below like weather. "I looked it up," Alex said. "The Rand formula. Justice Ivan Rand, 1946, after the Ford strike in Windsor, Ontario. Everyone covered by the contract pays, not just members." Nowak studied him, deciding something. "And?" Alex shifted his weight. "And I still don't know if it's fair that I pay for something I never chose. But I found out tonight that I'd be choosing it anyway, if it came to February." He hadn't meant to say that much.

"Nothing gets decided in stairwells," Nowak said. He put a hand on the rail, then took it off. "Come February, you'll know what your dues bought. One way or the other, you'll know." He pushed open the door to the street, and Alex heard the door below bang shut, then Margot's voice calling his name from the parking lot.

activity: to read an ocean current map and explain how the Gulf Stream warms northern Europe
knowledge_domain: to read an ocean current map and explain how the Gulf Stream warms northern Europe
fact: On many ocean current maps, warm currents are drawn with red arrows and cold currents with blue arrows.
story:
The outreach table had been Mr. Gupta's idea, a folding thing draped with a bedsheet and weighed down at the corners with wet sand, and Vincent had agreed to it partly because it counted for extra credit and partly because Noemie had agreed first. Their assignment was to stand on the beach beside a laminated ocean current map and explain to any passing stranger why northern Europe stayed warmer than its latitude deserved. Nobody had warned them that strangers on a beach do not want to learn things.

Jagger arrived late, carrying a slushie the color of a stop sign, and planted himself in front of the map with the confidence of a boy who had skimmed the reading. "This part's easy," he said, tapping the North Atlantic. "The red arrows are the fast ones. Blue means slow." A man in a bucket hat paused, looked at the map, looked at Jagger, and said, "Huh," in a way that suggested he had now been educated.

Vincent had his doubts, though he could not yet say where they came from. He crouched and studied the arrows. The red ones ran up along the coast of North America and across toward Europe; the blue ones curled down the eastern side of the Atlantic. If red meant fast, then the ocean was fast on one side and slow on the other, which was possible, he supposed, but the pattern looked less like traffic and more like something with a direction to it. He traced the red arrows with one finger and noticed that they all seemed to be moving away from the tropics. The blue ones moved back toward them.

"That's not speed," he said quietly. "I think red means warm. Blue means cold."

Jagger took a long pull of his slushie. "It's a map, not a mood ring."

"Think about it, though. Why would Mr. Gupta ask us why Europe's warm if the answer was speed?" Vincent felt the shape of the argument before he could finish it, which was usually how his worst mistakes started, so he tested it. He pulled up the reading on his phone, found the legend, and there it was in small print beside a red arrow: warm current. Beside the blue: cold current. He held the screen out. Jagger looked at it, then at the horizon, then said nothing, which for Jagger was close to an apology.

Noemie, who had spent the morning watching them instead of the map, knelt down next to Vincent. "So the red one going northeast, that's the Gulf Stream. It carries warm water up, and Europe gets the benefit." She said it lightly, checking, and Vincent nodded, though a knot remained. He understood that warm water was going toward Europe; he did not fully understand how water that begins near Florida ends up mattering in Norway, whether the warmth was carried like cargo or handed off like a rumor. He decided to be honest about the gap rather than paper over it, mostly because the bucket hat man was still within earshot and Vincent did not want to vilify the entire profession of science communication by guessing out loud.

The next visitor was a woman with two wet children hanging off her arms, and when she stopped, Vincent gave it a try. "Warm currents are red on these maps, cold ones are blue," he said, tapping the arrows. "So this red one is the Gulf Stream, moving warm water north and east, and that's why places like Britain and Ireland are milder than you'd expect that far north." The woman nodded, said "Oh, that's actually interesting," with genuine surprise, and one of the wet children asked whether sharks used the red arrows too. Vincent said probably, and the child accepted this as settled law.

Mr. Gupta came by near the end of the afternoon, sandals in hand, trousers rolled to the knee. He listened while a teenager in a populist T-shirt, some band or movement Vincent didn't recognize, argued that currents were invented by textbook companies. Mr. Gupta did not argue back; he asked the teenager where he thought the sand went when the tide dropped, and left him to chew on it. Later, walking the wrack line as the light turned crepuscular and the lifeguard chairs went dark, Vincent told him about Jagger's speed theory and admitted he still couldn't account for the whole mechanism, only the direction and the warmth.

"Good," Mr. Gupta said. "That's where the real question starts." He pointed at the water, where the last red of the sky lay on the swell like something being carried somewhere. "Tell me what you'd measure first."

activity: applying to college and waiting for the answer
knowledge_domain: applying to college and waiting for the answer
fact: The Common Application, which lets US college applicants send one application to many schools, was founded in 1975 with 15 member colleges and now has more than 1,000 members.
story:
The envelope had been sitting in Jake's backpack since Tuesday, and by Thursday it had begun to feel radioactive. He knew it was thick, and everyone said thick meant acceptance, but he refused to take it out at home, where his mother would hover, or in the hallway, where Simona would narrate. So he carried it into fifth period, Ms. Sow's classroom, and put it face down under his binder like a card he wasn't ready to turn over.

Ms. Sow was trying to get them to care about the League of Nations, which was a hard sell at nine in the morning. "Institutions," she said, writing the word on the board, "are just agreements people keep repeating until they forget they could stop." Jake copied it down without thinking, then looked at what he'd written, because something about it snagged. He raised his hand.

"Were there colleges in it?" he asked, and half the room laughed, and Ms. Sow didn't laugh, which was one of the reasons he liked her.

"The League had member nations," she said. "Some institutions have member colleges. Interesting that you ask, actually." But she didn't explain, she never did, she just said, "Skylar, you filled out your applications this fall. Tell Jake what you used."

Skylar spun around in her seat, which she did whenever she was permitted to talk. "The Common App," she said. "One application, and you send it to however many schools you want. It started in 1975 with fifteen member colleges, and now it has more than a thousand."

"Fifteen," Jake said. That number wouldn't leave him alone. Fifteen schools had once been enough to agree on something, and now a thousand of them were bound into the same form, the same essay prompts, the same little boxes for his activities. He tried to imagine the people at those first fifteen colleges, in 1975, deciding to trust one another's paperwork. How did an agreement like that grow from fifteen to a thousand? Did everyone just keep repeating it until they forgot they could stop?

"Why are you looking like that?" Simona whispered. She was the one who had dragged him to the college info sessions in the first place, back in September, when he'd been planning to work at his uncle's shop and see what happened. She had looked at him with actual pity, as though "see what happens" was a noxious gas leaking from his mouth.

"I got a letter," he whispered back.

Simona went still in a way she almost never did. "From where?"

He didn't answer, because Ms. Sow was passing out a worksheet, and because he honestly didn't know how to explain the situation. Here was the problem he hadn't told anyone: the letter was from a state school, a good one, with a scholarship offer that would burnish nothing on paper but would cover almost everything in reality. His mother had already taken a second shift. His uncle had already promised him a wage that felt, some nights, like recompense for every year his father hadn't been around. And there was a second envelope, or there would be, from the reach school, the one Simona had made him apply to, the one nobody from his neighborhood went to, and he was supposed to want that one more.

"Ten minutes on the worksheet," Ms. Sow said, and then, quieter, because she had eyes like a hawk and no apparent respect for a boy's privacy, "Jake, you have a letter in your backpack. I can tell because you keep touching the corner of it. Do you want the hallway or do you want to do it here?"

He had planned to wait, possibly forever. But there was something about the room, the radiator ticking, Skylar still half-turned in her seat, the word institutions drying on the board. An agreement people keep repeating until they forget they could stop. Maybe waiting was like that. Maybe he'd been repeating it so long he'd forgotten it was a choice.

He slid the envelope out and opened it with his key, along the top, the way he'd seen people do in movies. It was, in fact, thick. It was, in fact, acceptance, and the scholarship line was in bold, and Skylar said, very softly, "Oh my God," and Simona grabbed his wrist and squeezed it hard enough to hurt.

"So that's it," she said. It wasn't a question, but her face made it one.

"Here's the thing," he said, and his voice came out steadier than he expected. "This is the safe one. The other one doesn't come until March." He looked at the letter, then at her, then at Ms. Sow, who had retreated to her desk with the tact of a person pretending to grade. "Everyone keeps telling me the reach school is the prize. But this one says yes now. This one is real. And I keep thinking, fifteen colleges started that application thing, just fifteen, and it turned into a thousand, and maybe that's how everything works. You say yes to what's in front of you and it gets bigger than you planned."

"That's not how you're supposed to do it," Simona said. "You're supposed to wait for all of them and compare."

"I know how I'm supposed to do it."

"So what are you going to do?"

Ms. Sow looked up from her grading. Skylar had turned all the way around now. Outside the window the January light was doing its thin gray best, and the letter lay open on the desk between the worksheet and his binder.

Jake picked up his pen and signed the top of the acceptance form, then stopped with the pen still on the paper.

"Can a person sign in pencil?" he asked the room.

activity: to analyse a population pyramid to predict whether a country will need more schools or nursing homes
knowledge_domain: to analyse a population pyramid to predict whether a country will need more schools or nursing homes
fact: A pyramid with a wide base and narrow top shows a high birth rate and a young population, pointing to a growing need for schools and teachers.
story:
The library computers were all taken except the one by the window, where the radiator clanked and the afternoon light made the screen hard to read. Megan tilted the monitor and pulled up the two files Mr. Haddad had sent her after last period: population pyramids for Niger and for Japan, side by side, bars stacked in five-year bands like the specimens she'd pinned in biology last fall, each one filed into its phylum, its class, its order, as though a person's age could be sorted the way you'd sort a beetle.

She needed a decision by Friday. The service club had raised enough money to send two volunteers somewhere over spring break, and the coordinator had asked each applicant to write half a page on where the group's money would do the most good. Lilia wanted to go where the photos would be, which meant the orphanage in Japan that had been in the news. Megan hadn't been able to stop thinking about the other option, a school building project in Niger that had no photos at all, just a paragraph and a request for teachers.

"You're frowning at bars," Allan said, dropping his bag on the chair beside her. He had a free period and had apparently decided to spend it here. "Is that the volunteer thing?"

"Look at this." She turned the screen toward him. "Niger's pyramid. See how it's actually a pyramid? Wide at the bottom, narrow at the top."

Allan leaned in. "And Japan's looks like, I don't know. A top. Like a spinning top. Fat in the middle."

"Right." She tapped the base of Niger's chart, the longest bars, the ones for children. She had read the caption three times and the shape was beginning to mean something she couldn't quite say yet. A wide base and a narrow top, she thought. That's a lot of young people. That's a country full of kids. She traced the bars upward with her finger, watching them shrink. "So a pyramid like this, wide base, narrow top, that's a high birth rate. A young population. Which means..." She stopped, because the next part she was only guessing at.

Mr. Haddad came by on his way to the copier and paused behind them. He looked at the screen for a moment, said nothing, and kept walking, which was how he answered most questions if you hadn't asked one yet.

"Which means what?" Allan said.

"Which means it's going to need schools. Teachers, classrooms, all of it. Look how many kids there are under fifteen compared to everyone over sixty. It's not even close." She opened the second file and set Japan beside it, and the difference was so stark it almost exhilarated her, the way a proof does when the last line lands. "And Japan. Narrow base. The bars get wider as you go up, then thin out at the very top. Fewer kids than grandparents."

"So Japan needs nursing homes."

"Maybe. But Lilia's orphanage is in Japan."

Allan pulled the second chair around and sat. "So that's the problem?"

"That's the problem." She turned back to the screen. She wanted to say the answer was obvious, that the numbers pointed one way and she should just write it up, but the orphanage application had come with a letter from a woman named only as the director, describing children who had lost their grandparents in the last year, and Megan had read it twice and then closed the tab because it was hard to think with it open. Data on one side, a letter on the other, and she was supposed to weigh them in half a page by Friday.

"Here's what I don't get," Allan said. "The building project is already funded for the classrooms. It says so. They need teachers. Can our money even hire teachers?"

She hadn't noticed that. She scrolled through the paragraph again and there it was, a line about teacher recruitment being handled by the national ministry, the classrooms being the unfunded part. So the money would buy walls, not people. She wrote it down in her notebook, then crossed out half of it, then wrote it again. "Okay, so the pyramid tells me Niger needs schools. It doesn't tell me whether our two thousand dollars is the right piece of that."

"Could you split it?"

"Half a classroom." She laughed, but not really. The question underneath the question was whether she was choosing a country or choosing a project, and she had been treating them as the same thing all afternoon. The pyramid was about the country. The letter was about the project. Two different scales, and she had only one page.

Lilia arrived twenty minutes before the bell, out of breath from the far wing, and read over both their shoulders before Megan could close anything. "You're picking Niger."

"I don't know yet."

"You're literally pointing at the kids." Lilia tapped the wide base of the chart. "Look at it. It's all kids."

"I know what it shows," Megan said, more sharply than she meant to, and then softened, because Lilia wasn't wrong. "That's the country's future. Schools and teachers, that's what a shape like this points to. A wide base, narrow top, high birth rate, young population. It needs more schools. That part I'm sure of."

"But?"

"But I'm not sure our money is what closes the gap. And I'm not sure a place with an aging population doesn't need help too. The chart doesn't rank suffering. It just counts people."

Lilia was quiet for a second. "So write that."

"Write what, exactly? 'The data is equivocal'?"

"Write that you're sure about the schools and not sure about the money, and say which risk you'd rather take." Lilia shrugged, as though it were obvious, as though it weren't the entire question. "Pick the thing you can live with being wrong about."

The bell wouldn't ring for another quarter hour. Megan opened a blank document, typed the date, and stopped. Then she went back to the pyramid, to the long bars at the bottom, and counted them again, year by year, all the children arriving into a country that would have to find room for them. She set both charts side by side one last time and left them on the screen while she began to type.

activity: applying to college and waiting for the answer
knowledge_domain: applying to college and waiting for the answer
fact: Starting with applicants for 2026 entry, UCAS replaced the free-form personal statement with three structured questions about why the applicant wants the subject and how they have prepared.
story:
Claire's cousin had written her a two-page email about the personal statement, subject line "read this before you touch anything," and for three days Claire had not touched anything. The email said to open with an anecdote, to build a paragraph of narrative arc, to end on something that circled back to the beginning. Rosie had got into Durham with this method two years ago, and she had underlined the word method, which in an email meant italics, which meant she was serious.

On Thursday evening Claire finally sat down at the kitchen computer, the one with the desk lamp that flickered if you bumped it, and logged into her application. She had collated everything she thought she might need into one document: the draft she'd written in June, the notes from Mr. Fraser about voice and sincerity, a list of books she had half-read and could plausibly have finished. The document was called "statement stuff final v4." It was not final. It was not even v4, really, since v3 had been deleted in a fit of August self-loathing.

The screen did not look the way the email had described. There was no single box waiting for four thousand characters of her best self. There were three boxes. She counted them, then scrolled up and down as though a fourth might be hiding, then read the headings again. Three questions. One asked why she wanted the subject. Another asked how she had prepared for it. She read the third twice and sat back in the chair until the lamp flickered.

She texted Amir first, because Amir applied to medicine and knew things, then Elianna, because Elianna admitted to knowing nothing and would say so quickly, which saved time. Amir replied with a link and one sentence: "yeah it changed for 2026 entry." Elianna replied with a picture of her own screen, three boxes, and the message "is this a personality test." Claire called Amir and put him on speaker.

"So Rosie's whole thing," Amir said, "the anecdote, the arc, all of it, that's for the old format. They scrapped the free-form personal statement. Now it's three structured questions." He sounded almost cheerful, which Claire attributed to the fact that he had found out in September and she had found out now, in the second week of October, with a deadline standing behind her like a man checking his watch.

"The email is two pages," Claire said. "Single-spaced. She put the anecdote in bold."

"Frame it."

"Hang on, my mum's here." Her mother had come in with tea and was reading the screen over her shoulder in the way of mothers, half interested, half reconnaissance. "It's three questions now," Claire told her. "Not one big essay. They changed it."

Her mother nodded slowly, the nod of someone filing this under things that were different in her day, which was everything, and left the tea. On the phone Amir was still talking about the third question, the one about preparation, the one Claire had read twice because it seemed to want evidence. Not feelings, not an anecdote about the time she'd watched a documentary about cells and wept, but evidence.

She opened the old draft anyway. It began with a memory of her grandfather's garden, which had nothing to do with biochemistry except that both involved things growing under conditions of neglect. It was good writing. Mr. Fraser had said so, and Mr. Fraser did not say so often, and when he did say so it was with the reluctance of a man distrusting his own generosity. She read the first paragraph, and it was like holding something friable, a leaf skeleton, beautiful and past holding together; if she tried to move it into the new boxes it would come apart into phrases that meant nothing on their own.

Here was the trouble, and she turned the chair to face it. Rosie's method assumed one audience and one continuous act of persuasion, a single hall where you arranged yourself in the best light from the best angle. The three questions assumed something else: that the admissions tutors had got tired of the arranging. They wanted the why and the how separated out, like a form at a doctor's surgery, and the artfulness would have to go somewhere else, or shrink, or disguise itself as plainness. Claire suspected, though she could not prove it, that the second way was more honest and less true. A person was not actually three questions. A person was a garden with a grandfather in it, and the new format had no box for grandfathers.

She called Mr. Fraser the next morning, at the classroom door before registration, because emailing him felt like handing over a problem she had not yet tried to carry. "My cousin's advice is out of date," she said. "The statement's three questions now."

"I know," he said. "I've been telling the Year 12s since September."

"You didn't tell us."

"You finished in June. You had the old form." He looked at her for a moment with something between sympathy and arithmetic. "How much of your draft was anecdote?"

"Some." The tea was still in her hand, going cold, a prop now. "Most. All of it, honestly."

Mr. Fraser said, "Then you have the harder job, ironically. The students who never wrote the essay don't have to unwrite it." He held the door. "Bring me the three answers on Monday. And Claire, don't check the veracity of everything Rosie says, just the things with dates on them."

That weekend she cut the draft apart. The garden went into question one, compressed to two sentences, the grandfather reduced to a clause, and it was somehow truer for being smaller, like a specimen under glass. The reading list, cleaned of every book she had abandoned at page sixty, went into question two with the summer course and the hospital volunteering and the fact that she had kept a lab notebook for a fermentation experiment that had failed and smelled appalling, and which she now described, in the driest possible prose, as instructive. The third answer she wrote last, and it was the shortest, and she could not decide whether that meant it was the most honest or the least.

She hovered over the submit button for a while, which was itself a kind of waiting, a preview of the waiting to come, and then she pressed it, and the screen told her her application had been received, and that decisions would follow in due course, a phrase that meant anything and therefore nothing. She texted Rosie a screenshot of the three boxes with no message attached.

Rosie replied in four minutes. "What site is this? Mine didn't look like that."

activity: applying to college and waiting for the answer
knowledge_domain: applying to college and waiting for the answer
fact: Early Decision in US college admissions is binding: a student admitted with acceptable financial aid must enroll and withdraw all other applications.
story:
The coffee shop smelled of burnt milk and cinnamon, and Alexa had spread the Common App across the small table by the window as if it were a map she could fold differently. Saif set down two hot chocolates and slid one toward her, then sat, unpeeling his scarf.

"You changed the deadline question again," he said, reading upside down. "It still says November first."

"It says I haven't decided anything." She turned her laptop so he could see the admissions page, the gold banner across the top. "Early Decision. Binding."

"My cousin did that," Saif said. "If they take you and the financial aid is okay, you have to go. You have to pull every other application."

"Every single one."

"That's what binding means, apparently." He sipped his drink. "So apply."

Alexa looked out the window. Parker was crossing the parking lot with a folder under her arm, waving through the glass before she even reached the door. She had been accepted to two state schools already, with merit scholarships printed on thick paper, and she carried the folders around the way other people carried phones.

"You're doing the ED thing," Parker said, dropping into the third chair. "I can tell by your face."

"My mother keeps saying I'd be crazy not to. Better odds, done by December, no spring of waiting."

"And?"

"And I don't know what aid looks like anywhere else. That's the whole problem. If I apply Regular Decision, schools send offers, and I compare them. If I apply Early Decision and they admit me with aid I can accept, there's nothing to compare. There's no other offer, because there are no other applications."

Parker opened her folder of thick envelopes, then closed it, as if realizing what she was doing. Saif stirred his chocolate slowly.

"The school has a net price calculator," Alexa went on. "It says my family would pay about what my mother said we could. About. But a calculator is a calculator. Parker's offers are pieces of paper with real numbers, and mine would be one piece of paper, and if the number were even a little wrong, I'd still have to say yes. If it's okay, I have to enroll. That's the deal."

"Then don't do it," Parker said. "Wait like the rest of us. April is survivable."

"My mother thinks waiting is how you lose. And she's not entirely wrong. The admitted rate is better early." Alexa pulled the laptop back and looked at the gold banner again. "Mr. Brown would say there's no trick here, just a trade."

Mr. Brown, who taught her economics class, was in fact two tables away with a crossword, and he raised his pencil without looking up. "I heard my name."

"Nothing," Alexa said, and he smiled at his newspaper.

Parker leaned in, lowering her voice. "Okay, but here's what I think you're doing. You're pretending the trade is symmetric, and it isn't. Your mother's version is all about getting in, like getting in is the prize. Your version is about the four years after getting in. Those aren't the same game."

"That's very quotable," Saif said.

"I've been thinking about it since September."

Alexa had been thinking about it since September too, though not in those terms. Her mother talked about the competitive school the way her grandfather had once talked about land, the oldest son getting the whole farm, everyone else making do. Primogeniture, her history teacher had called it last spring, and her mother had laughed, unoffended, because in her family the eldest daughter had in fact inherited everything worth having. The habit of aiming everything at one prize was old, older than the application system, and Alexa had absorbed it without noticing. It felt almost anachronistic now, applied to financial aid forms.

She closed the laptop halfway, then opened it again.

"Here's where I actually am," she said. "I'm not choosing between my mother's way and Parker's way. I'm choosing whether the certainty is worth the blindness. If I go Early Decision, I'm betting that the calculator is right and that the school's aid will be acceptable, and if I win the bet, I get December instead of April. If I go Regular, I keep every option and pay for it in months of waiting and slightly worse odds. Both of those are defensible. What I can't do is pretend one of them is safe."

"So which one?" Saif asked.

"Regular. Probably. I want to see the actual numbers before I sign anything binding. But I'm honest that I might be wrong, and being wrong means I gave up the better odds for paperwork."

Parker pushed one of her thick envelopes across the table. "Keep it. For the December you won't be having."

Alexa took the envelope and squared it against her laptop, then began unclicking the November first deadline on her screen, the cursor hovering over the change before she pressed it.

activity: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
knowledge_domain: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
fact: Kwanzaa, created by Maulana Karenga in 1966, runs from December 26 to January 1 and honors seven principles, one each day, beginning with Umoja, meaning unity.
story:
The community hall smelled of fried plantains and floor wax, and Alice had eleven minutes to figure out what she was going to say. Her aunt had cornered her by the punch bowl an hour ago with the Kinara candles already waiting on the stage: "You're eighteen now, baby, you're doing the explanation tonight." Which was how Alice found herself at a folding table, flipping through a photocopied pamphlet while her little cousins staged a sword fight with plastic spoons behind her.

"Having a crisis?" Trent slid into the chair beside her, stealing a mandazi off her plate. He'd come as her guest because his own family was three states away and, as he put it, free food was one of the few remaining honest pleasures in this world.

"I've been asked to explain Umoja and I have approximately nothing." Alice tapped the pamphlet. "I know it's today's principle. That's the full extent of my knowledge."

"That's chicanery," Trent said. "Making you present without a syllabus."

"It's not chicanery, it's tradition." But she was laughing, and then Kason dropped into the third chair, out of breath, having apparently run from the bus stop in December without a proper coat. Kason had done a whole school project on Kwanzaa sophomore year and now regarded himself as the leading authority in any room containing a Kinara.

"Don't tell me," Kason said. "They asked you to do the principle thing."

"December 26th," Alice said, checking her phone. "Umoja. Unity. That's where I am."

"Okay, so." Kason held up one hand, obviously delighted to expatiate. "Maulana Karenga created Kwanzaa in 1966. It runs from December 26 to January 1, seven days, and each day honors one of seven principles, one per day. Today's the first. Umoja. It means unity."

Alice wrote it down, fast, before he could pick up speed. Kason's explanations were like rivers; you had to dam them early.

"See, I thought it started Christmas day," Trent said.

"Everyone thinks that. It's the day after." Kason leaned back, chair creaking dangerously. "You could just say all that and sit down."

"No, she can't." Ms. Sultani, who ran the hall's Saturday language classes and had apparently been eavesdropping with the serene confidence of someone who had raised four children, set down a cup of punch. "Anyone can recite a fact. The aunties will nod politely and forget it by the rice." She looked at Alice. "What does unity actually ask of you?"

"That sounds like a trap," Alice said.

"It is a trap," Ms. Sultani agreed, and walked away, sipping her punch.

Alice sat with it. The thing was, she had two ideas pulling at her, and they didn't fit together neatly, and she suspected the aunties would want them to. One was the obvious one: unity as warm togetherness, everybody at the same table, spoons and cousins and all. The other was harder. Last summer her grandmother had stopped speaking to her brother over something neither of them would name, and at Thanksgiving the empty chair had been papered over with extra dishes, everyone performing a unity that wasn't real. Unity that's only performance is just a nicer word for pretending. But unity that demands you never disagree with family is its own kind of cage; it can turn sectarian, us sealed off from them, loyalty mistaken for love.

Nine minutes. Eight.

"Okay," Alice said, standing, smoothing her skirt. "I'm going to say it's about choosing each other on purpose. And that Karenga built it first, on day one, because you can't do the other six without it. And that it's hard and sometimes it fails, and when it fails you notice the empty chair." She looked at Trent. "Too heavy?"

"For this crowd? They'll weep." Trent pointed to the stage, where her aunt was already beckoning with both hands and a luminous smile. "Go before she does the whistle."

Alice crossed the hall. The candles were lit, the mkeka laid out, and the room went quiet in that particular way rooms do when they expect something. She took the microphone, heard it pop, and found Kason in the back row giving her a thumbs up so large it was practically sectarian in its allegiance to her personally.

"December 26th," she began. "Day one of seven. Umoja, which means unity."

Her grandmother, in the second row, looked up from her lap. Alice took a breath.

"So. There's an empty chair at my grandma's table."

activity: to plan a weekly training program for a sport with rest days and warm-ups
knowledge_domain: to plan a weekly training program for a sport with rest days and warm-ups
fact: In periodized training, a season is divided into cycles; a microcycle, the smallest, usually lasts about one week.
story:
Cameron arrived at the community pool at six in the morning with a spiral notebook and the sense that he was about to be found out. The coach had handed the notebook back to him on Friday with one sentence written across the top: "Where are the rest days?" He had planned seven straight days of sprints, because he wanted the record more than he had ever wanted anything, and seven seemed like the number that matched wanting.

He sat on the wet concrete of the bleachers and watched Adalyn swim her warm-up, slow laps that looked, to him, like wasted time. She was fast, though. Faster than him, if he was honest, which he was trying to be this summer. When she pulled herself out at the wall, she came and dripped onto his notebook.

"Still no rest days?"

"He wrote it like an injunction. Like a commandment."

"It kind of is one." She flicked water off her fingers. "You swam hard Monday through Wednesday and then had a turgid, awful workout Thursday. I watched you. Your strokes looked like you were swimming through soup."

"That's not why. I just slept badly."

"Sure."

Hubert came out from the locker room with his phone in his hand and his towel around his neck, and he had that expression he got when he'd been reading something and wanted to be asked. Cameron didn't ask. Adalyn did, because she was better at that.

"It's this site Hubert found," she said, reading over his shoulder. "It splits the season into cycles. Big ones, then smaller ones."

Hubert turned the screen toward Cameron. There was a diagram, boxes nested inside boxes, and in the smallest box, the word microcycle. "The smallest one usually lasts about a week," Hubert said. "Coaches call it a microcycle. The week, I mean."

"So my week is already a thing."

"Your week was always a thing. You just planned it like it wasn't."

Cameron took the phone and looked at the diagram for a long moment. He had been thinking of training as a wall he could build higher by adding one brick every single day, but the page in front of him suggested something else, that a week was itself a unit, shaped on purpose, with effort folded into recovery like a sentence folded around a pause. He had assumed rest was the absence of work. The diagram treated it as part of the work.

"It's still one fact," he said. "It doesn't tell me what to do Monday."

"Then decide," Adalyn said. "You're the one who wants the record."

He opened his notebook to a fresh page. The old plan sat on the left like an accusation. He copied the week across, Monday through Sunday, and then, with the pen hovering, he compartmentalized it, hard days in one column, easy days in another, and left Sunday blank except for one word: nothing. On Monday and Thursday he wrote warm-up, 400 easy, before the sprints, because if Adalyn's slow laps were what fast looked like at the start, then his old habit of diving in cold and immediately going hard was not toughness. It was just bad arithmetic.

"Saturday's still hard," he said, showing Hubert. "Two days before the meet."

"You're supposed to taper, probably."

"I'm not tapering. I'm resting. There's a difference."

"There's really not," Adalyn said, but she was smiling, and she took the pen out of his hand and drew a small sun in the Sunday square, the way you would on a calendar, on a day worth marking.

The lifeguard blew the whistle for the six-thirty lane assignments, and Cameron closed the notebook, stood, and pulled his cap on. Whether the plan would work, whether the rest would buy him the half-second he needed, he could not know yet, and he was surprised to find that not knowing felt less like a failure than it had on Friday. It felt like a week. He stepped to the edge of the lane, put his goggles on, and pushed off slow, easy, counting the length, saving everything.

activity: saying goodbye to a grandparent who has died
knowledge_domain: saying goodbye to a grandparent who has died
fact: During China's Qingming Festival, which falls on April 4, 5 or 6, families visit their ancestors' graves to sweep and clean them and leave offerings of food.
story:
The kitchen still smelled of her grandmother's ginger, though the spice tin had sat unopened for eleven days. Samantha stood at the counter with a shoebox of things the hospital had returned: reading glasses, a hairpin, half a roll of peppermints, and an envelope with Samantha's name in the careful, upright script that had labeled forty years of school lunches. Inside was a single sheet. "For Qingming," it said, "you know where the broom is."

She did not, in fact, know. She knew the word only as a sound her grandmother had used each April, usually while dusting something that didn't need dusting, and Samantha had never asked, because at fourteen and fifteen and seventeen she had been busy, and asking would have cost her an afternoon. Now the afternoon stretched in front of her with nothing in it but the funeral that was over and the casserole dishes neighbours kept leaving on the porch.

Maelys came over at noon, still in the black tights from the service, carrying a paper bag of clementines because she never arrived anywhere empty-handed. She read the note twice, frowning at the broom mention as if it were a riddle to be litigated. "Qingming," she said slowly. "My roommate's family does it. It falls on April fourth, fifth or sixth, one of those days, and families go to their ancestors' graves. They sweep and clean the graves, and they leave offerings of food."

"On the graves," Samantha repeated. Her grandmother was an hour's drive away in ground that was still too new to have grass on it, and Samantha had a physics test tomorrow, and the car was technically her mother's. She said none of this. Instead she opened the spice tin, and the smell rose so suddenly that she had to put her palm flat on the counter.

The summer she was ten, her grandmother had let her sweep the porch with the real broom, not the toy one, and had called every wobble of the handle a peccadillo, laughing at the word until Samantha laughed too, though she hadn't known what it meant. "Small sins," her grandmother had said finally, wiping her eyes. "Small crooked sweeping. Nothing that matters." Then she had taken Samantha's hands and shown her how to pull the strokes straight, how the dirt gathered itself if you stopped fighting it. Samantha had thought that was the whole lesson: sweep properly, or don't bother.

Now she wondered whether her grandmother had been doctrinaire about the broom, or about April, or about anything at all, or whether she had simply wanted company in the ritual and never said so in a way a girl would hear. "She put it in writing," Samantha said. "She never put anything in writing." Maelys peeled a clementine and handed her half, which was how Maelys argued: quietly, with fruit.

They cooked. It was not graceful. Samantha found her grandmother's recipe for the long noodles, the ones she'd made every birthday, the ones that meant long life, and she understood with a small cold shock that her grandmother had been handing her a language the whole time and she had treated it as dinner. The water took forever. Maelys chopped scallions crooked, and Samantha said, "peccadillo," and they both went quiet, and then Maelys said, "exactly," and kept chopping. They swept the kitchen floor even though it was clean, Samantha pulling the strokes straight, and set a bowl of noodles at her grandmother's place at the table, where the chair had not been moved.

Her mother came in from the porch with a casserole, stopped in the doorway, and looked at the bowl for a long moment. Samantha waited to be told it was silly, or sweet, or to be asked whether she intended to drive out to the cemetery tomorrow after her test, which she was suddenly, without deciding to, intending. Her mother set the casserole down without answering either question and went to the drawer for a fork.

"We can't be sure she'd have wanted the noodles over the flowers," Samantha said. "She never said which she counted more." Maelys considered this, orange peel curling in her fingers. "Then you sweep anyway," she said. "Just in case it's both." Outside, the April light lay long across the floorboards, and Samantha picked up the broom.

activity: to interview for a part-time job with confident eye contact and clear answers
knowledge_domain: to interview for a part-time job with confident eye contact and clear answers
fact: Eye-contact norms differ: steady eye contact often signals confidence in North American interviews, while in some East Asian settings prolonged direct gaze at a senior person can seem impolite.
story:
Morgan had the interview scheduled for four o'clock, which meant she had exactly one bus ride, twenty-two minutes of potholes and diesel smell, to become a different person. She sat in the third row from the back with her knees against the seat in front of her and a folded practice sheet of interview questions in her lap, and across the aisle Kim was reading the sheet upside down.

"You look like you're being interrogated," Kim said. "Loosen your shoulders."

Morgan loosened her shoulders and they crept right back up. "My mom did a mock interview with me last night. She said I keep dropping my eyes, like I'm guilty of something."

"So look at the person. Easy."

"That's what she said. Stare them down, basically. She said in an interview here, the one who looks away loses." Morgan tried it out on Kim, a steady unblinking hold, and Kim laughed so hard a junior two rows up turned around.

Then Guneet climbed on at the second stop, saw the papers, and dropped into the seat beside Morgan before anyone could explain. She understood within a minute anyway, because Guneet's aunt had been coaching her too, for the same mall job fair, and here was the strange thing: Guneet's aunt had told her the opposite. Don't hold the manager's eyes, her aunt had said. It comes across wrong, like you're challenging them. Look at the table sometimes, let your gaze settle elsewhere, show respect that way. Guneet had been practicing a soft, drifting sort of attention on the bus window all week, which Morgan had assumed was daydreaming.

"Wait," Morgan said. "So my mom says look, and your aunt says don't. They can't both be right."

"They're both right," Guneet said, with the certainty of someone who had already argued this out at a dinner table. "My aunt says steady eye contact with a senior person can seem impolite. Where she grew up. My cousin got told off at a bank for it once."

"That's insane," Kim said, from across the aisle, not unkindly, just with the flat conviction of someone whose whole family agreed on eye contact.

Morgan looked at the practice sheet. The questions seemed suddenly like the easy part: why do you want this job, tell me about a time you worked in a team. She could answer those. The hard part was something nobody had written down, a code she'd never noticed she was following. She thought about how her mom straightened up when the vice principal walked past, and how her grandmother, when she visited, kept her eyes on the teapot while she said exactly what she meant. Two women, both certain, both correct in their own rooms. What would it mean to be correct in a room you'd never entered, with a manager whose face you couldn't predict?

"Here," she said to Guneet. "Watch my face. I'm going to try something in between." She let her eyes hold Guneet's while she answered a practice question, why do you want to work at the garden centre, and then, at the natural pause between sentences, she let her gaze drop briefly to the sheet before lifting it again. Not a flinch. Just a comma, a place to rest. "That," she said. "Was that weird?"

Guneet considered it with actual gravitas, chin lifted, like a judge at a diving competition. "That was fine. You looked like you were thinking, not like you were scared."

Kim leaned into the aisle. "Do it to me. I'll be the manager." She arranged her face into terrible authority, one eyebrow up, and Morgan ran through three questions that way, holding, resting, holding, while the bus jolted over the rail crossing and the practice sheet nearly went under the seat. The window Guneet had been staring through went by in a blur of fields, and Morgan noticed something she hadn't before: Kim broke eye contact constantly, glancing at the ceiling, at her phone, at nothing, and nobody in her family would call that rude. It was just how Kim was. Maybe, Morgan thought, the rule wasn't one rule at all but a whole quiet negotiation that people were doing all the time without naming it.

"Question," Kim said, still in manager voice. "Where do you see yourself in five years?"

"Employed," Morgan said, and Guneet snorted, and for a second the whole thing, the sheets and the aunt and the mother and the unknowable manager, felt less like an exam and more like a thing you could be curious about. There was a kind of gravitas, Morgan decided, in admitting you didn't know the code and were going to listen for it anyway. The real interview would tell her something the practice couldn't: whether the manager wanted to be looked at like her mom said, or spared the full force of it like Guneet's aunt said, or didn't care, like Kim.

The bus pulled into the mall loop and the doors sighed open. Morgan stood, folded the sheet into her jacket pocket, and Guneet squeezed her elbow once, an ancillary sort of gesture, small but somehow invigorating, like a corner of a pep rally compressed into a hand.

"If it goes wrong," Guneet called after her, "tell me which way it went wrong."

Morgan stepped down onto the curb, looked straight at the glass doors, then, halfway across the parking lot, let her eyes rest a moment on the plant displays in the garden centre window before lifting them again.

activity: to check a viral video's source and date with a reverse image search before sharing it
knowledge_domain: to check a viral video's source and date with a reverse image search before sharing it
fact: A video cannot be reverse-searched directly by most image engines, so fact-checkers take screenshots of key frames and search those images instead.
story:
Coralie found the video at 7:14 in the morning, before her bus came, and by lunch she had watched it eleven times. The clip showed men in waders dragging a heron out of a reed bed, its wings pinned, the water brown and sluggish behind them, and the caption said it had happened that weekend at the millpond, two kilometres from the school, because the council was about to pass an ordinance letting developers "clear" the wetland. Three hundred people had shared it from her town alone. Her thumb hovered over the share button in the computer lab, the fan humming under the desk, the room smelling of warm dust and floor cleaner.

"Don't send it yet," Tenzin said, leaning over from the next station. He had a way of saying things like that, quiet and infuriating. "If it's real, it'll still be real in an hour."

"That's the most privileged thing I've ever heard," Coralie said, but she lowered the phone. She wanted it to be real, she realized, which was a strange thing to want about a suffering bird. She wanted the outrage, the petitions, the reason to march past the town offices with a hand-lettered sign.

She pasted the video's link into an image search and got nothing useful. She tried again with different phrasing, chewing the inside of her cheek, while Jeffery watched from across the aisle with his chair tipped back.

"Have you tried searching it with your feelings?" he said. "Very effective."

"Be facetious somewhere else."

"I'm being helpful. I'm keeping you calm."

Ms. Krause came past on her rounds, checking that nobody had spilled juice on the keyboards again, and paused at the drowning-photo wallpaper of a wetland on Coralie's screen. "I reverse-search things all the time," she said. "Old postcards. I found one of this building from 1971 last spring." She moved on before Coralie could ask her anything, which was, Coralie later decided, the whole point of Ms. Krause.

The video itself wouldn't search, that was the problem. It sat there like a locked box, four hundred and six seconds of it, and Coralie was about to give up and share the thing out of pure spite when Tenzin reached over and tapped the screen. "You can't search a video," he said. "Fact-checkers take screenshots of the key frames and search those instead. The images. You search the pictures."

So she scrubbed through the clip and caught the frames that mattered: the men's faces, the licence plate on the truck, a glimpse of a road sign half-hidden by reeds. Print Screen, crop, paste into the search bar. The first two frames gave her nothing but stock photos of wetlands and an ad for binoculars. The road sign frame, when she ran it, returned a page from a news site, and the page loaded slowly, the lab's connection dragging its feet, and Coralie sat with her hands flat on the desk while the images resolved one by one.

It was the same sign, the same reeds, the same men. The story was from six years ago, from a different country, a licensed bird rescue during a canal dredging, the heron oiled and being saved, not taken. The millpond ordinance was real, Coralie knew, she had read the council minutes herself, but the video had nothing to do with it. Somebody had resuscitated old footage and dressed it in her town's name, and three hundred people, including half her follow list, had believed it because they wanted to.

She typed the correction slowly, attached the screenshot of the original article, and posted it. By the end of the day the video's shares in her town had dropped, and so had two of her friendships, the group chat going quiet in that particular silent way, one person typing "thanks for ruining it" before leaving. Jeffery found her at the bus loop with her bag over one shoulder.

"Turns out the heron was fine," she said.

"I saw." He kicked at a clump of dirty snow. "The ordinance hearing's still Thursday, though. Tenzin's making signs. Ugly ones."

She looked at the frozen puddle by the curb, the ice cloudy and ridged like the surface of a pond, and pulled her pen out of her bag. "Then give me the poster board."

activity: to find the derivative of a polynomial function and use it to locate a maximum
knowledge_domain: to find the derivative of a polynomial function and use it to locate a maximum
fact: At a local maximum of a polynomial the derivative equals zero, because the tangent line at the top of the peak is horizontal.
story:
The bell over the door of Mr. Levy's corner store had been broken for a month, so Maria announced herself with the squeak of the third floorboard, the one Sameer had identified on day one as the store's alarm system. She set her binder on the counter beside the register, next to the tray of expired chocolate he sold at half price, and pulled out the worksheet she had been failing at since dinner.
