"Closing in forty minutes," Mr. Levy said, not looking up from his crossword. "Then I lock the till, and you two solve your problems on the curb."

"Nine minutes," Sameer said. He was already at the little table by the window where the morning papers got stacked, spreading out his notes with the ceremony of someone setting a table for guests. "I've got nine minutes of dignity left before the exam, and you're going to give me every one of them."

The exam was at eight the next morning. Maria had spent the evening telling herself she understood the material, an approach her mother gently called her study heuristic: if you feel prepared, review once more, and if you feel doomed, review twice. Tonight she felt doomed, which by her own rule meant she had dragged Sameer here after his shift and spread out the profit problem Mr. Levy's nephew had supposedly failed two years ago: sketch a company's profit as a polynomial, then find the day the profit peaks.

"The sketching is fine," Sameer said, drawing the curve with his pen tilted almost flat, a smooth hill rising and falling across the graph paper. "It's the locating the peak that kills me. I keep guessing by eye. Look, the top's somewhere here." He tapped a point near the crest, where the curve was almost level, and his finger landed a full unit to the left of where Maria's did when she tried the same trick.

"You're both guessing," Mr. Levy said. He had abandoned the crossword. "My nephew did the same thing. Eyeballed it, got it wrong, and his teacher eulogized his effort in front of the whole class. 'He tried so hard,' she said, which you children should know is the sound of a failing grade being read aloud politely."

Maria laughed, but the laugh dried up when she looked at the curve again. Somewhere in the week's notes there had been something about slope, something she'd half heard while copying the homework off the board. She flipped back through her binder, past the smudged graphs, until she found it: the derivative, written out for a simple polynomial, a rule for turning a function into its own slope. She didn't understand why the rule worked, only that it did, and at the moment that was enough.

"Okay," she said, and worked it out on a napkin because the graph paper was full. She took the derivative of the profit polynomial, term by term, checking each against Sameer's notes while he narrated anxiously over her shoulder. Then she set the result equal to zero and solved. "When the slope is zero. That's the point where it flattens out. And at the top of the peak the tangent line is horizontal, so the slope there is zero, so..." She plugged the value back into the original function and got a number that landed, when Sameer marked it on the sketch, exactly at the crest of his curve.

"At the maximum," Sameer said slowly, "the derivative equals zero." He looked at the napkin, then at the graph, then at the napkin again, as though expecting them to disagree. "So you don't have to guess. The algebra tells you where the top is."

"Ten minutes," Mr. Levy said, and began stacking the chocolate tray.

They tested it on a second curve, a valley this time, and the method found the bottom just as cleanly, which Maria found both satisfying and slightly suspicious. The slope was zero at the peak and at the valley and, according to one of Sameer's margin notes, at points that were neither, which meant the algebra pointed at every flat place and left you to judge which one mattered. She said so, and Sameer, who had spent twenty minutes defending his eyeball method, nodded and crossed out the little X he had penciled on his original guess. "I was wrong," he said. "You were right, and I hate it, and tomorrow we're both going to be right."

Mr. Levy unlocked the door for a woman buying milk, then held it open for them, napkin and all. "Leave the graph paper," he said. "My nephew comes in Saturdays. He should see it."

Maria folded the napkin along the crease the derivative had made through her handwriting and put it in her pocket, next to her bus pass, where she could feel it through the fabric all the way home.

activity: going on a first date
knowledge_domain: going on a first date
fact: In the law of many jurisdictions and in consent education, consent to any intimate contact can be withdrawn at any time, even after it was first given.
story:
The rink smelled of cold rubber and burnt sugar from the snack bar, and Zoe laced her skates with the focus of someone defusing something. Felix-Antoine was already on the ice, doing slow laps near the boards, and watching him glide made her stomach tighten in a way she couldn't classify as pleasant or otherwise. They had been paired on a chemistry project in the spring, and he had asked her out on Tuesday with the sentence "Do you want to maybe do something," which had metastasized in her mind over four days into a whole imagined evening, then a whole imagined autumn.

Nyah had talked her through it on Friday, sitting cross-legged on Zoe's bed with a bag of sour candies. "You know consent isn't a contract, right," Nyah had said, not looking up from her phone. "Like even if you say yes to something, you can take it back. Any time. Even after you already said yes." Zoe had rolled her eyes and said obviously, but the words had lodged somewhere and refused to be dislodged, the way a song does.

Mr. Çelik, who ran the rink and had taught Zoe's learn-to-skate class when she was nine, sharpened a blade at the counter and gave her a look. "You're shaking," he said. "Cold or nerves?" She said cold. He said nothing, only slid the mittens she'd forgotten in the lost-and-found box across the counter toward her, mittens she recognized because she'd lost them in February.

The first half hour was better than she'd feared. Felix-Antoine was worse at skating than he pretended, and when he went down hard near the zamboni gate she laughed before she could stop herself, and he laughed too, sitting on the ice with his palms up, and something loosened between them. They bought hot chocolate. His hand found hers across the little table, and she let it stay, and that was fine, that was even good, his thumb moving in small circles over her knuckles while the overhead lights buzzed and the session clock counted down.

After, in the parking lot, the cold had teeth. He walked her toward her mother's car with their shoulders bumping, and when they reached the door he turned to face her and moved closer, and she understood with total clarity what was coming, and understood also that fifteen minutes ago she had wanted it. But the wanting had thinned somehow between the rink and the asphalt, the way heat does, and she found that her body had already stepped back before her mouth caught up.

"Can we not," she said. "Like, I know I was, earlier, holding hands and stuff. But I'd rather just say goodnight. If that's okay." Her voice came out smaller than she'd rehearsed.

He stood very still for a moment, and she watched him work through it, watched the disappointment cross his face and then, slowly, get set aside rather than allowed to curdle into something uglier. "Yeah," he said. "Of course that's okay." He put his hands in his pockets. "Text me when you're home?"

In the car her mother asked how it went, and Zoe said fine, good, actually, staring at the window while the rink's sign slid backward out of view. She thought about how Nyah's line had sounded like a rule, bureaucratic, almost a dysphemism for something tender, and how the thing itself was nothing like that. It was just true. She had said yes with her hand at the table and no with her whole body in the parking lot, and the no had counted, and nothing bad had happened, which felt both enormous and completely ordinary, a door that had been open all along and that she had finally walked through. Whether she would see Felix-Antoine again, whether the evening would retroactively become awkward in both their memories, whether wanting and not-wanting would always arrive this out of sync, she couldn't know yet, and she let the not-knowing sit beside her the whole way home like a third passenger.

From the driveway she texted him. "Home. Thanks for tonight." She watched the three dots appear, vanish, appear again, and then, before anything could arrive to replace it, she looked up at her own lit window, warm and square against the dark, and went inside.

activity: voting in an election for the first time at eighteen
knowledge_domain: voting in an election for the first time at eighteen
fact: CIRCLE, a research center at Tufts University, estimated that 50 percent of Americans aged 18 to 29 voted in the 2020 presidential election.
story:
Mr. Nkosi had pushed the desks into a crooked horseshoe, which he did whenever he wanted an argument instead of a lesson, and on the whiteboard he had written a single word: "Turnout." The room smelled of dry-erase marker and the radiator's burnt dust, and outside the window a flagpole rope clanked against the metal in a wind nobody inside could feel.

"Half of you will not vote," Mr. Nkosi said, not unkindly. "Statistically speaking."

"Half of young people," Tina said. "Not half of this room."

"Name your source," said Shelby, who had her laptop open and her thumb already moving toward the trackpad, a person for whom every disagreement was a citation away from settlement. "Because there's a research center at Tufts, CIRCLE, and they estimated that 50 percent of Americans aged 18 to 29 voted in the 2020 presidential election. Exactly half. Not most, not barely any. Half."

Jason had been listening with his chin on his fist, and the number settled oddly in him, the way a fact does when it refuses to flatter either side of an argument. Shelby was using it to say young people were negligent. Tina wanted to use it to say the system was broken. The number itself just sat there, unhelpful to everyone.

"Fifty percent," Tina said. "So my vote is basically a coin flip that cancels someone else's."

"That's not what a coin flip means," Shelby said.

"It's what it means to me."

Jason raised a hand he did not wait to be called on. "My dad didn't vote until he was thirty-one," he said. "He told me last night at the kitchen table, over meatloaf, like he was confessing to a crime. He said nobody ever asked him to. Nobody asked, so he didn't go." He paused, hearing how thin it sounded. "Somebody asked me. That's it. That's the whole difference. I'm not going to pretend it's more philosophical than that."

The night before, the polling place had been the fire hall two blocks from his house, and he had walked there in the dark with his registration card folded into a square so small it had become a lump. Inside, the volunteers had been two older women and a man in a hunting cap, and the ballot had been bigger than he expected, with races he had not studied, water commissioner, judge of the probate court, names that had coagulated into an alphabet soup on the sample ballot he'd skimmed in the car. He had voted for the things he knew and left blank the things he didn't, and the man in the hunting cap had fed his ballot into the machine and said, "There you go, young man," as though Jason had returned a library book. Walking home, the streetlight at the corner had buzzed and flickered, and Jason had felt, briefly and without drama, like someone who lived in a town that counted him.

In the classroom, Mr. Nkosi was nodding at Shelby's number with the caution of a man stepping around a wet floor sign. "So is fifty percent a tragedy or a triumph?" he asked. "Discuss among yourselves. I'll be pretending not to listen."

"Triumph," Tina said immediately. "In 2020, during a pandemic, half showed up anyway. That's stubborn."

"Or it's scathing," Shelby said. "Half of an entire generation looked at an election and stayed home. My brother stayed home. He had a shift at the warehouse and he said it wouldn't matter, and I'm still mad at him, and I'm allowed to be."

"Both," Jason said.

They both looked at him.

"Both, and I can't make it neater than that," he said. "Half of us went and half of us didn't, and I don't know which half I'm in on any given day, honestly. I voted last night. I left three races blank because I didn't know who the people were. So was I in the half that showed up, or only sort of?" He turned his pen over in his fingers. "I think that's what nobody wants to say. The line isn't between voters and non-voters. It runs through each of us."

"That's very liminality of you," Tina said, and then, when he squinted at her, "Mr. Nkosi used it in September. The in-between state. Doorways, graduations, waiting rooms. I remembered it because it sounded like a disease."

The bell was three minutes away and everyone's backpacks had already begun their slow migration toward the floor. Mr. Nkosi erased "Turnout" from the board and wrote nothing in its place, which felt, to Jason, like the most honest thing an adult had done all week.

"Where'd you vote?" Shelby asked, zipping her bag. "The fire hall?"

"Yeah. The guy with the hunting cap fed my ballot in for me."

"Romantic," Tina said.

"Extremely," said Jason, and he picked up his pen.

activity: to pass a driving test by practising parallel parking and merging on the highway
knowledge_domain: to pass a driving test by practising parallel parking and merging on the highway
fact: When parallel parking, a driver usually reverses in from alongside the car in front, turning the wheel toward the curb first and then away as the car swings into the space.
story:
The driving school shared a parking lot with the community college, and Michael had taken to arriving early so he could watch the cones before his lesson. There were five of them, spaced like the corners of a box, and he had a notebook in which he had drawn the box from above and labelled the gaps. His test was in eleven days. He had failed once already, on parallel parking, and the examiner's face had gone flat and unimpressed in the way that adults' faces do when they have decided something about you.

Mr. Pierre was the instructor the school assigned to him on Tuesdays, a small, deliberate man who wore the same grey cardigan regardless of the weather and spoke only when the car was stationary. Michael's mother called him garrulous compared to the last instructor, though in the car he was nearly silent, and Michael had learned to prefer this, because the silence left room for him to feel what the wheels were doing. In school Michael was the opposite; in Mr. Pierre's passenger seat he listened.

The problem was consistent and therefore maddening. Michael would pull up alongside the cone that stood for the car in front, reverse, turn the wheel toward the curb, and then keep turning toward it, as if more of the same motion would finish the job. Every time he ended up at an angle, the rear of the car too close to the curb and the nose swinging wide toward the imaginary traffic lane. He would correct, overcorrect, and sit there with his hands at ten and two, waiting for the verdict.

"You turn the other way," Mr. Pierre said one Tuesday, after the fourth attempt. That was all. Michael sat with it. He looked at his drawing in the notebook, the little arrows he had made showing the direction of the steering, and he understood, slowly, the way you understand a word you have read many times and only now hear spoken, that the turn toward the curb was only the first half. A driver usually reverses in from alongside the car in front, turning the wheel toward the curb first, and then, as the car swings into the space, away from it. The wheel had to come back. He had been treating one motion as if it were the whole motion.

"It's like a sentence," Maelle said at lunch the next day, when he was trying to explain it. She was applying to art schools and thought in terms of composition. "You start going one direction and then you turn. The turn is the point." Erin, who was studying for a statistics exam and thought in terms of procedures, disagreed. She said parking was not like anything, it was just parking, and the reason Michael kept failing was that he insisted on making things into metaphors instead of just doing them. "You could operationalize it," she said, tapping her review sheet. "Line up, reverse, turn in, turn back. Steps. Measure your distance from the curb after. If it's under a foot, it worked." Michael liked both of them and had privately begun to suspect that both of them were right, which was inconvenient, because their rightnesss pointed in different directions.

On the following Tuesday he tried Erin's way first. He said the steps to himself, out loud, in order, and on the second attempt the car settled against the curb with both sides even, and Mr. Pierre said "there," a single syllable that Michael found himself absurdly proud of. But on the next attempt, when he tried to repeat the steps exactly, a cone drifted somewhere he did not expect and he froze, because the steps had no line in them for a cone being in the wrong place. Real streets, he thought, were full of cones being in the wrong place.

So he tried Maelle's way, which was harder to describe and therefore harder to fake. He stopped reciting and watched the car's nose in relation to the curb, letting the shape of the manoeuvre decide when the wheel came back, and it worked twice and failed twice, and he could not yet say whether the failures were his or the method's. Afterward, in the school library, waiting for Maelle to finish her shift at the circulation desk, he wrote in the notebook: steps carry you until the situation changes; the turn carries you through the change; need both. It was not a conclusion. He underlined nothing.

The morning of the test, Maelle and Erin walked with him partway, one on each side, arguing mildly about whether encouragement helped or was, as Erin put it, a distractor with a friendly face, and Michael did not resolve it for them. He had his notebook in his jacket pocket. At the testing centre parking lot, the examiner, a woman with a clipboard and a cough drop she shifted from cheek to cheek, gestured toward the curb and the space between two cars and said, "Whenever you're ready." Michael pulled up alongside the car in front, checked his mirror, and began to reverse, the wheel already turning toward the curb, his hand waiting on it, ready to turn away.

activity: to analyse a population pyramid to predict whether a country will need more schools or nursing homes
knowledge_domain: to analyse a population pyramid to predict whether a country will need more schools or nursing homes
fact: A pyramid whose base is narrower than its middle shows falling birth rates and an aging population, pointing to rising demand for nursing homes and elder care.
story:
The travel agency sat between a dry cleaner and a shuttered phone repair shop, and Jackson had worked its Saturday shift for three weeks, mostly laminating brochures for places nobody booked anymore. His geography project was due Monday. He had spread the papers across the counter when Mr. Dlamini stepped out of the back office.

"Customers need that surface," Mr. Dlamini said, though the only customer so far had been a man who absconded with the free mints without asking about a single package.

"Ten minutes," Jackson said. "It's the last question." The sheet showed two population pyramids, side by side, one for Niger and one for Japan, bars of males and females stacked by age. Question four read: Which country will need more schools, and which will need more nursing homes? Explain using the shape.

Mr. Dlamini picked up the sheet anyway. He ran a thumbnail along the Japan pyramid, where the widest bars sat in the middle and the base below them narrowed to a smaller footprint than the bulge above. "I sell holidays," he said. "I don't sell homework." But he set the sheet back down, facing Jackson, and did not go into the office.

Tom arrived at noon with two coffees and his own copy of the assignment, folded into quarters. "I put nursing homes for Niger," Tom said, dropping onto the stool behind the second terminal. "Wide base, right? All those kids. Kids means schools. I flipped it."

Jackson looked at the Niger pyramid, wide at the bottom, tapering to almost nothing at the top. Then at Japan again, its middle fatter than its base, the whole shape narrowing where the youngest bars should have carried the future. "Wait," he said. "If the base is narrower than the middle, that's falling birth rates. Everyone's already old, and fewer people are coming up behind them. So Japan needs the nursing homes. Niger needs the schools."

"So I had it backwards," Tom said.

"You had it backwards." Jackson wrote it down, then stopped. The shape told him demand, but demand kept snagging on something else. He kept thinking about his grandfather's care home out past the ring road, how the staff on the dementia wing were nearly all his grandfather's age themselves, or close to it. He'd visited on Thursdays for two years and never once seen anyone under forty on that floor.

Donovan came in at two to mock Jackson for having a job at all, leaned over the counter, and jabbed a finger at the Japan pyramid. "That's grim," he said. "That's an upside-down country. Who's going to look after all that?"

"That's the part the shape doesn't tell you," Jackson said. "It shows you what the country will need. It doesn't show you who does it." He thought of Thursday again, of the agency's wall of posters, Thailand, Portugal, the Philippines, sun-bleached and curling at the corners, and understood for a second why Mr. Dlamini's business still existed at all. People moved. That was the other half of the answer nobody had asked for on the sheet.

Tom was already copying Jackson's paragraph in his own handwriting, faster than he could have worked it out himself. Jackson let him. There was a version of this where he said something, and a version where he didn't, and the one where he didn't felt like a small, quiet solipsism, a decision that only his own Monday mattered.

Mr. Dlamini emerged at closing with his keys. He looked at the pyramids one last time, still spread across the counter. "That second one," he said. "That is my country. When I was your age, the base was wide. Everyone had four, five children." He jingled the keys once and put them in his pocket. "Laminate the rest tomorrow. And put the mints behind the till."

Jackson stacked the sheets. On the bus home he looked at the window instead of his phone, at the housing blocks sliding past, and found himself doing the bars in his head, counting pushchairs against walking sticks, an arithmetic with no answer yet. He got off two stops early and stood outside his grandfather's home for a minute in the cold before going in, listening to a television somewhere below the ground floor, subterranean, faint, turned up loud for someone who could no longer hear it quietly.

The nurse at the desk was new, young, maybe twenty-five. "You're the Thursday grandson," she said, and held out the visitor book. "He's been asking whether you'd come."

activity: to compute the integral of a function to find the area under a curve
knowledge_domain: to compute the integral of a function to find the area under a curve
fact: In a definite integral the constant of integration cancels out, because it is added to both F(b) and F(a) and then subtracted away.
story:
Keira spread her returned test on the counter of Ms. Nasser's corner store, between the lottery rack and a display of pens that claimed to write upside down, and pointed at the red circle around her answer. "Minus two," she said. "Two whole marks, for a plus C."

Leon leaned over from the ice cream freezer, where he had been conducting a serious inspection of the popsicle selection. "Plus C is the whole point," he said. "Ms. Okafor drilled it into us. No plus C, no marks. Now she's taking marks off for it?"

"I wrote it on a definite integral," Keira said. "The one with the limits, from zero to two." She had done the rest of the question perfectly, drawn the little curve, shaded the strip of area she was hunting for, and then, in a final flourish of obedience, appended the constant like a signature. The red pen had circled it twice.

"Two dollars even," Ms. Nasser said, sliding a bag of chips across the counter. She kept a jar of stale licorice for students who came in looking penurious at the end of the month, and she had already begun twisting off the lid. "And a licorice, on the house, because you two look like the test ate you."

"The test spat on me," Keira said, accepting the licorice. "There's a retest tomorrow at lunch. Same material. And I don't even understand what I did wrong, which is the worst part. If it were arithmetic I'd know. But this is a rule I've never heard of."

Leon requisitioned a napkin from the dispenser by the coffee machine and laid it flat over the test paper, as if covering the wound. "Okay. Do it again. From zero to two. I'll watch." He had a way of making even studying feel like a heist they were planning together, and Keira, who had walked to the store precisely because her bedroom had begun to feel like a trap made of her own handwriting, pulled the pen from her pocket.

She worked the antiderivative, wrote F of two minus F of zero, and stopped. "Wait. Here's the thing. The plus C goes inside here somewhere. It's part of the function I found." She wrote it small, tentative: F plus C, evaluated at two. Then again at zero. She stared at the napkin the way you stare at a magic trick you've seen a hundred times and never once caught. "So I'd have F of two plus C, minus F of zero plus C."

Leon picked up a second napkin, drew a crude pair of scales, and set an imaginary C on each side. "It cancels out," he said. "You're subtracting it away from itself."

"It cancels out," Keira repeated. She said it slowly, testing the floorboards of the idea before putting her full weight on them. "It's added to both, F of b and F of a, so when you subtract, it's just gone." She crossed out the plus C on the napkin with a flourish so violent the pen tore through. "That's why it doesn't belong on a definite integral. It's not a crime, it's a ghost. It does nothing."

"That is deeply unfair of it," Leon said. "Sneaking in, doing nothing, leaving." He tried to steal a piece of her licorice and she slapped his hand with the napkin, which was satisfying in a way no answer key had ever been. Ms. Nasser, who had been restocking the lottery rack and listening with the expression of a woman who had heard forty years of homework solved over her counter, said nothing, only raised an eyebrow at the torn napkin.

Keira copied the problem onto a fresh napkin, clean, and did it in four lines. No plus C. The area under her curve sat there at the end, plain as the price of chips, and she understood something she couldn't quite say to Leon: that the constant wasn't wrong exactly, it was beside the point, and knowing the difference between wrong and beside the point felt like the actual thing she'd been studying all semester. She folded the napkin and put it in her pocket, next to the test with its red circle.

"Tomorrow at lunch," she said, "I get my two marks back, and then you're buying the chips."

"I'm buying nothing," Leon said, but he was already at the freezer again, sliding it open.

activity: to plan a weekly training program for a sport with rest days and warm-ups
knowledge_domain: to plan a weekly training program for a sport with rest days and warm-ups
fact: The '10 percent rule', never raising weekly running distance more than 10 percent, is a popular guideline, but studies have not shown it prevents injuries better than other gradual plans.
story:
Owen found the whiteboard behind the Zamboni bay on Tuesday, half hidden under a stack of cones, and by Thursday he had claimed it. He wrote Monday at the top, then ice session, then the word rest, and stopped. Around him the rink ticked and settled, the compressors humming under the ice, the overhead lights making pale rectangles on the surface where the mites had just finished their skate. He was sixteen and had never planned a week of anything before, and the blank squares under his pen looked like small rooms he had to furnish.

Konnor found him there with his phone out, comparing two schedules. "You're doing it wrong," Konnor said, not unkindly. He leaned past Owen and wrote 10 percent in the corner of the board. "Never raise your weekly distance more than ten percent. That's the rule. Levi's cousin does it for cross-country, and he never gets hurt."

"It's called the 10 percent rule," Konnor added, as though the name settled the matter.

Owen copied it down, because Konnor sounded certain, and certainty was scarce in Owen's week. He had taken on the off-season program because the coach had asked for a volunteer and no one else had raised a hand, and now eleven teammates were waiting for him to tell them when to skate, when to run the hill behind the rink, when to do nothing at all. The nothing was what he kept second-guessing. Rest days looked like laziness on paper, even when he wrote planned in parentheses beside them.

That night he sat at the kitchen table and drafted a message to Ms. Mwangi, who taught biology and had once run marathons, and who had told the class that asking a good question was worth more than a confident answer.

Dear Ms. Mwangi, he typed. I'm building the off-season schedule for the team. A friend says the 10 percent rule, never adding more than ten percent to your weekly distance, is basically a law and I should build everything around it. Is that right? Also, is one rest day enough, or two, and should the warm-up come before the run or the skate or both. Sorry for all the questions. Owen.

Her reply came before he had finished his dishes.

Owen, a good question is specific, and yours is. I won't answer it for you, but I'll tell you where to look. When you've read for twenty minutes, tell me what you found and what you still don't know. That last part matters most.

He read for longer than twenty minutes. He found running sites where the 10 percent rule was quoted like scripture, and then he found the studies, and the studies were quieter than the websites. The guideline was popular, everyone agreed on that much, but when researchers compared it against other gradual plans, plans that increased load carefully without the ten percent ceiling, it had not prevented injuries any better. He read the sentence three times. It did not say the rule was bad. It said it was not special. That was somehow harder to hold.

At the rink on Saturday he told Konnor while they laced up, the dressing room smelling of tape and old rubber. "I looked it up. The 10 percent rule is popular, but the studies haven't shown it prevents injuries better than other gradual plans. So it's a choice, not a law." Konnor rolled his eyes, but Levi, pulling his jersey over his head, said, "So any slow build works, as long as it's actually slow?" and Owen said yes, that was about the size of it.

They voted on it, a show of sticks in the change room, which Levi grandly called a plebiscite, and the team chose a plan of Owen's own: small increases, two rest days, warm-ups before every session, ice and running both. On the wall above the benches someone had taped an old poster from a field trip, a photograph of a montane forest, dark firs going up a grey slope, and Owen looked at it while the last players filtered out. He taped his finished schedule beside the poster, with rest days marked in green and a note that the body needed time to habituate to new load, which was a phrase he had liked and decided to keep. Under the whole thing he wrote, in smaller letters, we may change this in three weeks, and left his pen on the ledge beneath it. Konnor picked the pen up, added a small check mark, and skated out onto the empty ice.

activity: moving to a new town and leaving old friends behind
knowledge_domain: moving to a new town and leaving old friends behind
fact: Using 2007 survey data, the US Census Bureau estimated that a person in the United States can expect to move about 11.7 times in a lifetime.
story:
Gabriella counted the boxes in the truck bed one more time, as though the number might have changed since Ohio. Nineteen. Her mother climbed into the driver's seat and looked over the map on her phone, then at the house that was no longer theirs.

"Cheer up," her mother said. "You know the Census Bureau did a survey, 2007 data, and figured the average American moves about 11.7 times in a lifetime? This is just one of them."

"That's supposed to cheer me up?"

"It's supposed to make it ordinary."

It did not make it ordinary. It made it arithmetic, and arithmetic did not cover Alexis's face at the going-away party, or the way Maxime had hugged her and then walked off before she could say anything back, hands jammed in his pockets like he was protecting them from her. She couldn't verbalize any of it on the eleven-hour drive, so she watched the highway instead and did the math anyway. Eleven point seven moves. If her parents were on move number six or seven, then half her life had already been spent arriving and leaving, and the years ahead held four or five more of these goodbyes, evenly spaced like fence posts she couldn't see yet.

The new classroom smelled of floor wax and somebody's vanilla latte. Mr. Tanaka wrote his name on the board and asked them each to say where they'd come from and one thing they'd left behind. Most students said a town and a joke. When her turn came, Gabriella said, "Ohio. A treehouse my friends and I built in ninth grade," and sat down fast, because if she said anything truer her voice would go.

After class a girl with paint on her knuckles caught up with her in the hall. "Maxime?" the girl said, squinting at the schedule in Gabriella's hand. "Sorry, you just look exactly like somebody I follow online. Different name. Anyway, you're in my art block. I'm Alexis." She talked the whole way to the studio, which spared Gabriella the morass of small talk she always sank into with strangers, the weather, the school, the mascot. Alexis pointed out the vending machine that ate quarters, the stairwell that smelled like the pool, and then, in the studio, a half-built canvas frame leaning against the window. "That's mine. It's a mess. You can help if you want something to do with your hands."

Gabriella did want something to do with her hands. She held the frame steady while Alexis stretched the canvas, and when Alexis asked, idly, why she'd really moved, Gabriella found she could talk with her eyes on the pliers and the tacks. "My mom got a job. Eleven point seven times, that's what she says the average person moves. She thinks that means it's fine." Alexis pulled a tack tight and considered it. "Is she wrong?"

The question sat with Gabriella through lunch and into Mr. Tanaka's afternoon seminar, where he had them debating whether roots or movement made a person who they were. Students took sides loudly. A boy argued that anyone who stayed in one town their whole life was hiding; a girl argued that moving constantly hollowed you out. Gabriella, to her own surprise, raised her hand. "My mom says the Census Bureau, using 2007 survey data, estimated that a person in the United States can expect to move about 11.7 times in a lifetime. Everyone was arguing like it's a choice between staying forever and never staying. But that number is in the middle. Almost nobody gets either extreme." Mr. Tanaka didn't confirm or correct her; he only said, "So the question becomes what you do with the middle," and moved on to somebody else, which she understood was a kind of respect.

That evening she texted Maxime. She had drafted the message four times in Ohio and deleted it, but the frame of the day had changed somehow; Alexis's question had loosened something. "You walked away before I could say bye properly," she wrote. "I'm not over it. I don't know if I'll be back ever or when. But I keep thinking you build a treehouse and then you leave it standing, and that's not nothing." She stared at the message for a full minute before she sent it, because it was the truer thing and truer things cost more. Then she helped her mother carry box number twelve, the one with the dishes, into the kitchen.

His reply came while she was taping her class schedule to the wall above the desk. "Sorry. I'm bad at endings. Treehouse is still standing. Send pictures of wherever you are and I'll send some of it." Not resolved, not restored, but a thread left uncut. She set the phone on the windowsill and looked out at the strange dark street, the porch lights of a town that did not yet know her, and typed back, "Deal. First picture tomorrow, if the light's good."

activity: to write a research paper with an argument, footnotes and a bibliography in a standard citation style
knowledge_domain: to write a research paper with an argument, footnotes and a bibliography in a standard citation style
fact: MLA style cites sources in the text with the author's name and page number in parentheses, and lists the full sources at the end under the heading 'Works Cited'.
story:
Avery spread the photocopied articles across her bedroom floor like evidence at a trial she had not yet learned to prosecute. Her topic was the erosion of the littoral zone along the eastern shore, the narrow ribbon where land and water negotiated their terms, and she had opinions about it, too many opinions, none of them yet arranged into anything a reader could follow. Ms. Tesfaye had asked for eight pages with an argument, footnotes where they were needed, and sources cited properly, and had written one sentence on the assignment sheet that Avery had read four times without fully absorbing: the parenthetical citations and the final list would follow MLA.

At school the next morning, Philip leaned across the aisle of the history classroom with his laptop turned toward her. He was building a website, he said, drone footage of the shoreline, the bluffs, the houses leaning toward the water, and he meant to monetize it eventually, sell subscriptions to the sort of people who liked watching a coast disappear in high definition. "Look at my bibliography," he said. "Mr. Hall wants it alphabetical, and the footnotes go at the bottom of each page. Took me an hour to get the format right." Avery glanced at it, the numbered notes, the formal list titled Bibliography, and felt a small cold shift in her stomach, because her English draft, three pages in, was built the same way.

"I think MLA is different," she said slowly, and Philip shrugged, already back to trimming a clip of the collapsed stairway at Miller Point.

That evening Avery sat at the kitchen table while her mother washed dishes, and she pulled out the style guide Ms. Tesfaye had left on the class shelf. She followed the examples with her finger, sentence by sentence, and the system began to assemble itself in her mind. In the text, the author's name and the page number went in parentheses, right there where the borrowed idea appeared, so a reader could trace any claim to its source without leaving the sentence. Then at the end, the full sources were listed under a heading of their own, not Bibliography, not Sources. She said it aloud to the empty room, testing it. "Works Cited."

The next day she found Ms. Tesfaye erasing the board after last period. "I came from history class," Avery said, "and I kept almost writing a bibliography the way we do over there. But for your paper, it's Works Cited at the end, and the author and page number in parentheses inside the paper. Right?" Ms. Tesfaye smiled and said, "That's MLA," and handed her a sample paper from the folder on her desk, and Avery carried it home like a map of a country she had finally agreed to visit.

Rewriting the draft was slower than writing it had been. She had to decide, paragraph by paragraph, what actually belonged to her and what belonged to the engineer at the state office, to the geologist, to the councilman whose letter to the editor had called any restriction on seawalls a reactionary plot against property owners. She put his name and the page number in parentheses after his own words and let him stand there, cited and accountable. Where two of her sources disagreed about whether the shore could be saved by engineering or only by retreat, she discovered she could not pick a side cleanly, and she let that trouble show in a paragraph instead of papering over it, though she was not sure Ms. Tesfaye would reward the honesty.

Philip came over on Sunday with his drone in a padded case and a bag of clementines, because he knew Avery skipped lunch when she was working. He peeled one for her without being asked and set the segments beside her keyboard. "Did you finish?" he said. "Because I need a sentence from somebody who's actually read the reports. My subscribers think the whole beach is going next summer, and I don't think that's true, but I don't know how to say I don't know." Avery pulled up her Works Cited page and turned the laptop so he could see the list, then scrolled up to a paragraph where the geologist's name sat in parentheses with a page number, holding down a claim the way a stake holds down a tent. "That's how," she said. "You say who found it out, and then you say what you still can't."

He copied the citation down on the back of a grocery receipt, and Avery saved her file, and outside the window the light was going amber over the roofs, the tide somewhere beyond them doing its slow, indifferent work.

activity: moving to a new town and leaving old friends behind
knowledge_domain: moving to a new town and leaving old friends behind
fact: Sociologist Mark Granovetter's 1973 paper 'The Strength of Weak Ties' found that people often learned of new jobs through acquaintances rather than close friends.
story:
The moving van left at four, and by six Jade knew the shape of the new house: which floorboard complained, which window stuck, which room her mother had claimed as an office without saying so. School started Monday. She had one weekend to become a person who lived here, and no idea how that was done.

Saturday she walked the neighborhood to forestall the alternative, which was sitting in her empty room texting Marilou and Ross about how wrong everything was. Three streets over, a woman was wrestling a rolled rug toward a porch. Jade took the other end without being asked, mostly because the rug was winning. "You're the girl from the blue house," the woman said. "Siddiqui. I teach at the high school. Your mother bought my lemonade at the garage sale, which I should warn you was a betrayal, because that lemonade was old." They got the rug inside, and Ms. Siddiqui gave her tea that was not old, and that was the whole of the acquaintance.

Monday, school. The building was the same species as her old one, locker bays and bell schedules, but everyone in it had history she couldn't see. In third period a boy named Ross, not her Ross, this Ross apparently the only Ross in a hundred miles, cracked a joke about the cafeteria's florid mural of vegetables, and she laughed before she could stop herself, and he looked pleased, and then the moment closed over like water and she was new again.

What she wanted was small and specific: a job. There was a bakery two blocks from home with a HELP WANTED sign in handwriting so desperate it had been underlined twice. Her mother had said, gently, that they could manage without her earning, which was true and also beside the point. The job was not about money. It was about having a reason to be somewhere on a Saturday that wasn't her bedroom.

She applied in person Tuesday. The owner, unhurried, said he'd had eleven applicants. Marilou texted that this was discouraging, statistically speaking, and Ross texted a picture of himself holding a sign that said HIRE JADE OR ELSE, which was, he noted, deterrence, and which Jade screenshotted and did not send to the bakery because she wanted the job, not a restraining order.

Wednesday, Ms. Siddiqui stopped her at the corner. "The bakery," she said. "I put in a word for you. Mentioned you'd helped with my rug and that you seemed sensible, which in my book outranks experience." Jade thanked her, startled, and walked home turning it over. She had met the woman twice. Twice, and a rug, and tea. That was the entire foundation. It seemed like cheating. It seemed like the kind of thing that happened to other people, people with aunts in every town.

That night she found herself explaining it to Marilou over video, half apology and half wonder. "There's this thing," she said, hedging, "I think I half-remember from somewhere. This paper. 'The Strength of Weak Ties.' This guy Granovetter, 1973. He found people learned about new jobs through acquaintances more often than through close friends." Marilou frowned at her through the phone. "That's backwards." "I know. But the bakery called an hour ago. I start Saturday." Marilou was quiet for a second, then said, "So I've been useless to you this whole time," and Jade said, "No, you've been essential, you just can't get me a job," and Marilou said that was the worst compliment she'd ever received, and they were both laughing, and it was almost like being in the same room.

Saturday morning she tied on the apron the owner handed her, an apron that smelled like cinnamon and other people's mornings. Through the front window she could see the street where she had walked with no destination, the porch where the rug had been. She couldn't decide whether the lesson was that effort mattered or that luck mattered, whether she had earned this or been handed it, and she suspected the question was badly framed, that the truth was some mixture she couldn't separate out. She decided she was allowed not to know yet. Ms. Siddiqui came in at nine for bread and, seeing her, raised one eyebrow. "Sensible," she said, and took her change and left, and Jade turned to the oven timer already beeping behind her.
